original.thread_name: Mortality effect of adjunctive atorvastatin (relative_reduction) —
original.title: "Success" in Phase III is unlikely to be a mortality result, so the 10% mortality effect is not what a "success" would establish
original.hypothesis: The prior evidence is on surrogates (culture conversion, radiographic damage). A mortality-powered Phase III in DS-TB is probably infeasible. If Phase III is designed on a composite "unfavourable outcome" (failure, relapse, death) or on culture conversion, passing it says little about on-treatment death. CG's model multiplies p_success = 0.40 by a 10% mortality effect as if "success" meant "a 10% mortality reduction was demonstrated." A large share of the success probability mass probably carries a mortality effect near zero, or an effect never measured.
original.mechanism:
SROI is linear in relative_reduction × p_success. Suppose a fraction f of "success" worlds are surrogate-only successes with a true mortality effect of about r_s. Then E[r | success] = (1−f)(0.10) + f·r_s. With f = 0.5 and r_s = 0.03 (my assumption, not sourced), E[r | success] = 0.065. That is exactly at the threshold that pushes SROI below 2,000x. With f = 0.5 and r_s = 0, it is 0.05, a 50% cut.

Sample-size check (my own arithmetic, standard two-proportion formula, 80% power, α = 0.05 two-sided):
- At 4% baseline on-treatment mortality and a 10% relative reduction (4.0% → 3.6%), about 36,000 per arm, roughly 72,000 total.
- At 8% baseline mortality (an HIV-enriched population) and a 10% reduction, about 17,000 per arm.
- At 2% baseline mortality (typical of trial-selected HIV-negative cohorts, as I recall), the requirement is larger still.
No TB drug trial approaches this scale. A trial powered for a 10% mortality effect is therefore implausible, and any realistic Phase III is powered on something else.
suggested_evidence: The sample-size arithmetic is a logical argument. The 4% and 8% baseline mortality figures are illustrative assumptions; the Verifier should check actual on-treatment mortality in DS-TB programs (WHO Global TB Report cohorts) and in trials. On surrogate validity, I believe Phillips et al. and Wallis et al. found 2-month culture conversion to be a weak individual-level predictor of relapse. I cannot supply exact citations or numbers. I know of no evidence that culture-conversion speed predicts mortality. UNGROUNDED pending verification of the Phase IIc/III registry design.

evidence_found: The Phase IIB was open-label, and muscle pain was more frequent with atorvastatin (16% vs 5%) . This affects how much the 97% vs 85% result can be trusted, but it is not mortality evidence.
The registry notes the Phase IIB also showed reduced incidence of peripheral neuropathy . This is another non-mortality signal.
Nothing I found supports a 10% mortality reduction from human data. The Investigator's central point is therefore consistent with the registry record.
caveats: Sample size of about 36,000 per arm at 4% baseline and a 10% relative reduction:** VERIFIED. I recomputed it with the standard formula (80% power, two-sided α = 0.05) and got about 35,900 per arm.
About 17,000 per arm at 8% baseline:** VERIFIED. I get about 17,200.
"Larger still" at 2% baseline:** VERIFIED. I get about 73,000 per arm.
Baseline mortality assumptions (4%, 8%, 2%):** PLAUSIBLE. These are illustrative, as the Investigator said.
A five-country cohort of 23,799 adults on DS-TB treatment found
6% died during treatment .
A systematic review reported case fatality during TB treatment ranging from 1.8 to 33.3% .
I did not find a source for the 2% trial-cohort figure.

Prior human evidence is on surrogates:** VERIFIED. The atorvastatin Phase IIB (n=150) reported culture-negative results in 97% vs 85.1% and a larger reduction in chest X-ray severity score . The Phase IIC (STEP) lists time to sputum culture conversion, decline in chest X-ray severity score and lung function as outcomes in 440 patients. Mortality is not a primary outcome.

No mortality-powered trial is planned:** PLAUSIBLE. The registry describes Phase IIC as a pilot Phase III and says the Phase III will be fully international and multicenter . I found no Phase III endpoint definition.

Phillips/Wallis found 2-month culture conversion to be a weak individual-level predictor of relapse:** UNVERIFIABLE in this session. I recall Phillips et al. (AJRCCM, ~2013) making this argument, but I did not confirm it.
No evidence that conversion speed predicts mortality:** UNVERIFIABLE. This is an absence claim and I found nothing either way.
f = 0.5, r_s = 0.03, and "exactly at the threshold that pushes SROI below 2,000x":** UNVERIFIABLE. These are assumptions and depend on CG's model.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
The prior atorvastatin evidence is surrogate-only (culture conversion, chest X-ray score). A mortality-powered DS-TB trial needs roughly 17,000–73,000+ per arm, depending on baseline mortality and assuming a 10% relative effect. A "Phase III success" is therefore most likely a composite-unfavourable-outcome or surrogate success. The mortality effect conditional on success should be discounted toward the surrogate-only value r_s, which is unknown. Keep the f and r_s numbers as flagged assumptions, and drop the Phillips/Wallis claim unless it is separately checked. Strength: **large in direction, with unknown magnitude**. It is conditional on how CG's model defines "success."

original.thread_name: Mortality effect of adjunctive atorvastatin (relative_reduction) —
original.title: A large share of on-treatment deaths is unreachable by a weeks-scale host-directed adjunct, and shorter regimens shrink the headroom further
original.hypothesis: Deaths during DS-TB treatment are concentrated early and in people with advanced HIV, severe malnutrition, old age, or late presentation. Many die before an adjunct that modifies inflammation and lung damage over weeks could act. Others die from non-TB causes or from comorbidity (HIV-related disease, cardiovascular and renal disease, diabetes complications). A "10% relative reduction in mortality" applies the effect to all deaths, whereas only a subset of deaths is plausibly modifiable.
original.mechanism: Write r_eff = (fraction reachable) × (effect among reachable deaths). If 25–35% of deaths are unreachable and the effect among reachable deaths is 10%, r falls to 0.065–0.075. That is at or near the materiality line. A weaker effect among reachable deaths pushes it lower. The 4-month HPMZ regimen is a further issue. It shortens the treatment window and likely lowers the on-treatment lung-damage burden that statins are meant to reduce. Only the share of deaths attributable to slow bacterial clearance or immunopathology is left for the adjunct to address, and the absolute effect shrinks if the baseline mortality rate is lower.
suggested_evidence: Waitt & Squire 2011 (systematic review of deaths during TB treatment, mainly in Africa) is the obvious source for timing and causes. I believe it reports that deaths cluster early and in HIV-positive patients, but I cannot recall the exact fractions. Verify. Precedent from other adjuncts: corticosteroids reduced mortality in TB meningitis (Thwaites 2004), a specific anatomical form, but there is no analogous result for pulmonary DS-TB overall. The HPMZ-headroom point is my own inference. UNGROUNDED on exact figures.

evidence_found: Because early deaths dominate, the adjunct's window matters. Atorvastatin was given for 2 months in the Phase IIB and 16 weeks in the planned sub-study, so it overlaps the early-death period only partly, depending on onset of effect.
The 1.8–33.3% range shows that the reachable share depends strongly on setting and HIV prevalence. Any single 25–35% figure is therefore weakly grounded.
caveats: Waitt & Squire 2011, systematic review of death risk factors:** VERIFIED as a citation. It is Int J Tuberc Lung Dis 2011;15(7):871–885,

"A systematic review of risk factors for death in adults during and after tuberculosis treatment" . It is cited as reporting comorbidities as risk factors for TB deaths in areas with high TB incidence and HIV prevalence . Its early-clustering and "mainly Africa" details are UNVERIFIED.
Deaths cluster early:** VERIFIED from other sources.
In a US study,
48% of patients who died during treatment died within 30 days .
In a Taiwan series, most TB-related deaths occurred early (median survival 20 days) .
In another Taiwan cohort, underweight was associated with higher mortality only in the first 8 weeks .

Many deaths are non-TB or comorbidity-driven:** VERIFIED. In the Taiwan series, malignancy, liver cirrhosis and renal failure were independent predictors of all TB deaths , and deaths were classified as TB-related or non-TB-related.
HIV is a major driver:** SUPPORTED indirectly. ART cut mortality by 44–71% among HIV-positive TB patients .
"25–35% unreachable":** UNVERIFIABLE. This is an illustrative number, and I found no source for the share of deaths that is modifiable.
Thwaites 2004 (corticosteroids in TB meningitis):** NOT CHECKED. I recall it as a real NEJM trial showing a mortality benefit, but I did not verify it here.
"4-month HPMZ shrinks headroom":** UNVERIFIABLE. The registered ATORTUB regimens use the standard six-month course, and the popPK sub-study lists
2RHZE/4RH plus 16 weeks of atorvastatin . I found no HPMZ arm. If CG's model assumes HPMZ, that is an external premise I could not check.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
On-treatment deaths are early-clustered and often tied to advanced HIV, comorbidity and non-TB causes. A uniform 10% relative reduction across all deaths likely overstates the modifiable share. The decomposition r_eff = reachable fraction × effect among reachable deaths is logically sound. The 25–35% figure is **UNGROUNDED** and should be presented as a placeholder. Remove the HPMZ headroom claim, or flag it as UNGROUNDED, unless CG's model actually uses a 4-month regimen. Strength: **small-to-medium**, because the direction is well supported but the magnitude is not.

original.thread_name: Mortality effect of adjunctive atorvastatin (relative_reduction) —
original.title: Rifampicin induction structurally limits atorvastatin exposure in routine programs, and the trial exposure does not transfer
original.hypothesis: Atorvastatin is a CYP3A4 and OATP1B1 substrate. Rifampicin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer that also inhibits OATP1B1 acutely. The atorvastatin label (as I recall) says concomitant rifampicin should be co-administered simultaneously, because delayed administration after rifampicin gave significantly lower atorvastatin plasma concentrations. That is the OATP-inhibition-versus-induction trade-off. Simultaneous dosing temporarily raises exposure through OATP inhibition, but under chronic daily rifampicin the net steady-state exposure is uncertain and plausibly lower. Programs cannot guarantee simultaneous dosing, and the trial may have been run under supervised, optimized dosing that routine DOT or self-administration does not replicate. Interactions with ART add another layer. Protease inhibitors (ritonavir-boosted) raise atorvastatin exposure and myopathy risk. Efavirenz lowers it. Dolutegravir with doubled-dose-under-rifampicin is less relevant.
original.mechanism:
If the statin effect is exposure-dependent, realized relative_reduction scales with achievable AUC or lipophilic tissue concentration in lung lesions. Halving effective exposure could plausibly lower the effect by more than half if the dose-response is steep (unknown). An illustrative range for the multiplier is 0.5–0.8 on r. That is my guess, not derived from data. Magnitude uncertain; it requires a PK/PD model.

Transferability across statins is a related problem. If the prior positive human data are from pravastatin (hydrophilic, not CYP3A4-metabolized, so largely unaffected by rifampicin) or rosuvastatin (minimal CYP metabolism), they do not demonstrate atorvastatin efficacy under rifampicin. The Phase IIc is then testing an exposure-limited drug with a different PK profile from the one that produced the signal.
suggested_evidence: The atorvastatin label statement on rifampicin (verify wording). Kyrklund et al. 2004 reported a large reduction in simvastatin exposure with rifampicin, as I recall, but I cannot confirm the numbers, and simvastatin is not atorvastatin. I believe a Johns Hopkins group (Karakousis) ran pravastatin Phase IIa work and that StAT-TB used a different statin, but I cannot confirm which. The Verifier must identify the exact statin in the prior trial. UNGROUNDED on specific PK reductions for atorvastatin under chronic rifampicin.

evidence_found: A population PK–PD sub-study is registered. It covers atorvastatin 20/40/60 mg with 2RHZE/4RH:
16 weeks of daily atorvastatin at each dose . The Phase IIC registry says

PK-PD evaluation at different doses, correlated with outcomes, will be essential . The investigators themselves treat exposure as an open question, which supports the Investigator's concern. The sub-study could also provide the missing data.

If a Phase III used a rifapentine-based regimen (as "HPMZ" suggests), the rifampicin-specific label guidance would not map directly. Rifapentine is also a CYP3A4 inducer, but I did not verify its atorvastatin interaction.
caveats: CYP3A4 induction plus OATP1B1 inhibition by rifampicin, with a timing trade-off:** VERIFIED. The label cites the dual mechanism (CYP3A induction and OATP1B1 inhibition) .

Atorvastatin-specific PK:** VERIFIED. The label table shows that with rifampin and atorvastatin co-administered (7 days), AUC rose 30% and Cmax rose 2.7-fold; with doses separated (5 days), AUC fell 80% and Cmax fell 40% . Backman 2005 confirms the 80% fall: rifampin reduced atorvastatin acid AUC by 80% .
"Net steady-state exposure uncertain, plausibly lower":** CONFLICTING.
The label's 7-day co-administration data show plasma AUC maintained or increased, not decreased.
A review notes that the consequences of prolonged simultaneous statin–rifampin administration have never been investigated .
Another review says that after multiple doses, induction can overcome the OATP effect and AUC decreases .
Net: uncertain, which matches the Investigator's wording, but "plausibly lower" is not established.
Protease inhibitors raise atorvastatin exposure:** VERIFIED.
Tipranavir/ritonavir raised AUC 9.4-fold . The efavirenz-lowers claim is supported by the label's inducer wording: efavirenz and rifampin can lead to variable reductions .
"Prior positive human data may be from pravastatin or rosuvastatin":** LARGELY FALSE for the likely source.
The positive human data are atorvastatin. The ATORTUB Phase IIA/IIB used atorvastatin 40 mg daily for 2 months with standard of care .
A reviewer notes that rosuvastatin did not affect sputum culture conversion , so rosuvastatin is a null result, not a positive signal.
The pravastatin work is PK-only.

Trial exposure doesn't transfer to routine programs:** WEAKENED. ATORTUB was run with rifampicin-containing standard therapy, so any rifampicin-induced exposure loss is already embedded in the observed signal. The remaining issue is whether dosing timing and adherence differ in routine care. I found no evidence on that.
Multiplier 0.5–0.8 on r:** UNVERIFIABLE. It is a guess, as the Investigator said.
Dolutegravir comment:** NOT CHECKED.
critique.revised_hypothesis: Atorvastatin exposure under rifampicin depends on dosing timing: separated dosing cuts AUC by about 80%, while simultaneous dosing preserves or raises plasma AUC at 7 days. Net chronic-dosing exposure at the site of action (lung, hepatocyte) is **UNGROUNDED**. The atorvastatin label itself says the hepatocyte effect is unknown. Replace "Kyrklund 2004 (simvastatin)" with Kyrklund 2000 (simvastatin) and Backman 2005 (atorvastatin). Drop the premise that the positive human signal came from a different statin, because the Phase IIA/IIB was atorvastatin, so the signal was generated under rifampicin. The surviving concern is that routine-program dosing may not reproduce trial-condition timing and adherence, plus the ART interactions. Strength: **medium** (reduced from large), with magnitude unknown. A PK/PD model or the ATORTUB popPK-PD sub-study is needed.

original.thread_name: Mortality effect of adjunctive atorvastatin (relative_reduction) —
original.title: Winner's-curse and reference-class patterns imply the conditional effect should sit well below the surrogate-implied one, and r and p_success should not be independent
original.hypothesis:
A 10% conditional effect is probably anchored on promising early signals. Effect sizes that clear a statistical filter in small, early trials are systematically overestimated. In TB host-directed therapy, the track record is of surrogate or early-phase positives that fail to translate into outcome benefit. Examples: vitamin D (the Martineau 2011 culture-conversion signal in a genotype subgroup, with no robust outcome benefit in later trials as I recall), CC-11050, metformin and everolimus (the latter two I believe produced mixed or no clear clinical benefit). The Verifier should check each.

The independence assumption also fails. Draws where Phase II/III "pass" are exactly those with large estimated effects, so the posterior mean of the true effect, conditional on passing a surrogate threshold, is shrunk relative to the point estimate. Where trials are powered on surrogates, "passing" selects on surrogate noise as well as true effect.
original.mechanism: With a Bayesian shrinkage factor of 0.7–0.9 (an illustrative assumption), r falls to 0.07–0.09 from this effect alone. Modeling the joint distribution, i.e. a mixture of "real effect" and "surrogate-only or null" worlds, would give E[r × p_success] below the product of means if surrogate-only wins are common.
suggested_evidence: Winner's curse in selected small trials is a general statistical result (logical argument). The HDT reference class is partly recalled and needs verification of each trial's actual endpoints and results. Observational statin cohorts (Taiwan, Korea) suggesting lower TB risk or mortality are exposed to healthy-user and indication bias. I cannot cite specific papers confidently. UNGROUNDED on specifics.

evidence_found: (additional)**
The directly relevant statin reference class contradicts the "early positive signal" premise. Human surrogate data for statins in TB are null so far.
Rosuvastatin phase 2b: median time to culture conversion was 42 days in both arms (HR 1.30, 0.88–1.91, p=0.19).
Rosuvastatin had no impact on PET-CT changes.
StAT-TB (pravastatin, phase 2b) is registered as completed.
I found no results in this search.
Atorvastatin evidence in these results is preclinical.
In guinea pigs, atorvastatin and anti-TB drugs showed a synergistic bactericidal action.

So the 10% likely rests on preclinical and observational anchoring, not a winner's-curse-selected human trial. That is a different mechanism (translation risk and confounding) and arguably points to a larger downward adjustment than shrinkage alone.
An editorial notes there is no clear consensus on appropriate biomarkers or study endpoints for HDT trials.
This supports the surrogate-to-outcome concern in general terms.
caveats: Martineau 2011 vitamin D trial, culture-conversion signal in a genotype subgroup:** VERIFIED, but the framing needs correcting.
Median time to sputum culture conversion was 36.0 days with vitamin D and 43.5 days with placebo (adjusted HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.90–2.16, p=0.14).
The primary endpoint was therefore null.
TaqI genotype modified the effect (p-interaction 0.03), with a response only in tt-genotype patients (HR 8.09, 95% CI 1.36–48.01).
The tt subgroup estimate is very wide and imprecise, which is a textbook winner's-curse profile.
This was a post-hoc subgroup signal, not a Phase II trial that "passed" a filter.
No robust later benefit:** VERIFIED.
A meta-analysis found no shortening of time to sputum culture conversion overall (HR 1.04, 0.89–1.23).
A later trial also found that the tt genotype did not influence conversion, in contrast with the earlier report.
The subgroup effect was not replicated in that trial.
CC-11050 and everolimus "surrogate positives that fail to translate":** MISREPRESENTED.
The relevant trial is Wallis et al. 2021, a phase 2 trial in South Africa (NCT02968927).
It found both drugs safe and well tolerated, and they might have improved FEV1 recovery.
FEV1 was significantly higher than control at day 180 (CC-11050 6.30%, p=0.048; everolimus 6.56%, p=0.044).
There was no effect of CC-11050 on stable culture conversion, which the authors attributed to small sample size.
The authors called for further definitive studies.
I found no Phase III, so these drugs have not "failed to translate". They are untested at Phase III.
Safety and FEV1 were the endpoints, not mortality.
Metformin "mixed or no clear clinical benefit":** NOT SUPPORTED as stated.
What exists is mostly observational or preclinical work.
A scoping review describes pilot preclinical and observational research recommending metformin as an adjunct.
The impact of combining metformin with RHZE is described as still under investigation.
Metformin is therefore unproven, not a documented translation failure. I found no completed outcome RCT in these results.
Observational statin cohorts exposed to healthy-user and indication bias:** PLAUSIBLE (logical argument).
Population-based studies found statin use related to lower TB incidence.
I did not locate the specific Taiwan or Korea statin cohorts, so I could not verify them. A comparable Taiwan metformin cohort did find an association with lower TB risk.
Winner's curse as a general statistical result:** VERIFIED as standard theory (no search needed).
Joint-distribution claim, "E[r × p_success] below the product of means":** LOGICALLY CONDITIONAL.
The sign of the covariance depends on how p_success is defined.
If success is defined on a surrogate and surrogate-only wins exist, high p_success pairs with r≈0. That gives a negative covariance, so E[rp] is below E[r]E[p], as the critique says.
If p_success means success on a mortality-powered endpoint, real-effect worlds have both high p and high r. That gives a positive covariance and the effect reverses.
I could not inspect the CG model to see which applies.
Shrinkage arithmetic:** the 0.7–0.9 factor is explicitly an assumption, and 0.10 × 0.7–0.9 = 0.07–0.09 is arithmetically correct.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
- **Survives:** The 10% conditional effect is probably over-optimistic.
  - Early or subgroup estimates are upwardly biased.
  - Martineau 2011 is a valid example, but of a post-hoc subgroup signal that did not replicate.
  - Observational statin data are confounded.
  - r and p_success are unlikely to be independent, though the sign of the effect on E[rp] depends on how success is defined.
- **Removed:** The claims that CC-11050, everolimus and metformin are failed-translation examples. They are unproven, not refuted.
- **Added:** Human statin-in-TB surrogate trials (rosuvastatin) are null. None of them used atorvastatin.
- **Status:** The shrinkage factor is UNGROUNDED, an illustrative assumption. Direction: decreases. Magnitude: medium.

original.thread_name: Mortality effect of adjunctive atorvastatin (relative_reduction) —
original.title: Hepatotoxicity and myopathy add a negative tail, and the combined attenuations compound
original.hypothesis: Adding atorvastatin to rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide stacks hepatotoxic risk, and statins carry myopathy risk, higher when co-administered with some ART. In a population where fatal drug-induced liver injury is a recognized cause of treatment death, even a small excess hepatotoxicity-related mortality could offset part of the benefit. Small phase II trials cannot detect this.
original.mechanism: CG models only a non-negative effect. If the true distribution includes a harm tail, E[r] decreases. For example, 10% probability of net-zero or small negative effect contributes about −0.01 on a base of 0.10, which is a modest and not threshold-crossing effect alone. The bigger issue is compounding with Critiques 1–4. Using my illustrative ranges (all assumptions, and they overlap): reachable fraction 0.65–0.75, PK attenuation 0.5–0.8, shrinkage 0.7–0.9. Product 0.23–0.54, so r ≈ 0.023–0.054 vs 0.10. Treat this as an upper-bound illustration, since CG's 10% may already partly embed some attenuation and the factors are correlated.
suggested_evidence: Hepatotoxicity of first-line TB drugs and statin liver and muscle warnings are well established in labeling. I cannot cite a study quantifying excess hepatotoxicity from statin plus HRZ co-treatment. The compounding calculation is my inference. UNGROUNDED on magnitude.

evidence_found: (additional)**
StAT-TB chose pravastatin partly for lower toxicity.
Pravastatin showed the least toxicity in THP-1 and Vero cells.
The programme's own choice of statin was driven by interaction and toxicity concerns.
The rosuvastatin trial's safety result is mildly reassuring but underpowered for mortality.
caveats: HRZ hepatotoxicity and statin liver/muscle warnings are well established:** PLAUSIBLE from standard labeling and general knowledge. I did not retrieve labels in this session.
Supportive data point: in the Wallis HDT trial, two control-group patients had life-threatening, treatment-attributable liver injury on standard therapy.
Small phase II trials cannot detect excess mortality from hepatotoxicity:** PLAUSIBLE (statistical).
The rosuvastatin trial is a data point.
Grade 3–5 adverse events occurred in 9% (6/70) with rosuvastatin versus 6% (4/67) in controls (p=0.75), none considered related to rosuvastatin.
There was no signal, but the trial is too small to exclude a rare harm. Rosuvastatin also has less CYP3A4 involvement than atorvastatin, so it does not transfer directly.
Myopathy risk higher with "some ART":** PLAUSIBLE but of limited relevance.

From my own knowledge (not searched here), the main statin interaction is with boosted protease inhibitors and cobicistat. Those are generally avoided with rifampicin, and efavirenz or dolutegravir regimens are the usual choice.
The ART argument is therefore weaker for rifampicin-based TB treatment.
"CG models only a non-negative effect":** UNVERIFIABLE. The CG model is not available to me.
−0.01 contribution:** arithmetic is correct (10% × 0.10 = 0.01).
A "net-zero" outcome is already what a failed Phase III in p_success represents. Counting it again as a harm tail risks double-counting.
Only the genuinely negative portion is incremental.

Compounding product:** arithmetic VERIFIED. 0.65×0.5×0.7 = 0.23 and 0.75×0.8×0.9 = 0.54, so r ≈ 0.023–0.054. The inputs come from other critiques that I cannot see. The Investigator itself flags that the factors overlap and are correlated.
PK attenuation (0.5–0.8):** this concerns rifampicin induction of atorvastatin metabolism.
I did not search this specifically. I know from general pharmacology that rifampicin lowers atorvastatin exposure, but I did not verify the magnitude here.
Supportive indirect evidence: the Wallis trial substituted rifabutin for rifampin because of potentially deleterious pharmacokinetic interactions with the HDT drugs.
The StAT-TB protocol cites known pravastatin–rifampin interactions in humans.
Interaction-driven dosing problems are a recognized concern in this field.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
- **Survives:** A harm tail for hepatotoxicity or myopathy is plausible and not testable in small trials. Adding hepatotoxic risk on top of HRZ is biologically coherent. Compounding of attenuations is a reasonable concern.
- **Corrections:**
  - The harm-tail adjustment is small (≈ −0.01 at most) and may double-count p_success.
  - The ART-myopathy point is weak for rifampicin-based regimens.
  - The 0.023–0.054 range is an upper-bound illustration. It uses correlated inputs from other critiques that could not be checked.
- **Flag:** "UNGROUNDED – plausible but needs empirical support" on magnitude. Direction: decreases. Magnitude: small for the harm tail itself, medium for the compounding.

original.thread_name: Realism of all-in cost (all_in_cost) — Phase III trial size,
original.title: A $7M Phase III cannot be powered on mortality, and the CEA's benefit is mortality only
original.hypothesis: The CEA's benefit stream is mortality reduction, assumed at 10%, and the model credits only mortality. A Phase III that produces guideline-grade evidence of a mortality effect of this size is a very large trial. Even a pragmatic, low-cost one is likely to cost several times $7M for the Phase III alone. If $7M instead buys a surrogate-endpoint trial (culture conversion, unfavourable composite outcome, relapse), the cost is plausible but the evidence does not support the mortality benefit being claimed. CG would then be either understating cost or overstating p_success. The two cannot both be right.
original.mechanism:
all_in_cost rises, and SROI falls in proportion to 1/cost.
- Own sample-size calculation (standard two-proportion formula, 80% power, α = 0.05, two-sided). Assume 5% baseline mortality and a 10% relative reduction, from 5.0% to 4.5%. That needs about 28,000 per arm, roughly 57,000 in total.
- With 8% baseline mortality, as in higher-risk or HIV-heavy cohorts, it is still about 17,000 per arm, roughly 35,000 in total.
- At a pragmatic cost of $500–$1,000 per participant, the trial costs about $17M–$57M. At conventional TB-trial per-participant costs, which I believe are in the thousands of dollars (UNGROUNDED), it costs more.
- Enriching for high-mortality groups (TB meningitis, advanced HIV) shrinks N. But it makes the evidence non-generalisable to the drug-susceptible (DS) majority that drives the 3.3M-patient benefit base.
- Central estimate for the Phase III alone is about $25–40M, with a range of $15–100M. Total all-in cost is then about $30–45M. SROI is about 3,000 × 7/37 ≈ 570x, with a plausible range of roughly 300–1,000x. That is a 3–10× reduction, far above the 25% materiality bar.
suggested_evidence: Logical and arithmetic argument, labelled as my own inference. The sample-size numbers depend on the baseline mortality and effect size, which the Verifier should recompute.

The cost-per-participant figures are UNGROUNDED. I believe the RECOVERY trial showed that very low per-patient costs are possible in a streamlined pragmatic design, but I cannot cite a specific figure.

I cannot cite a specific source stating what endpoint WHO's Guideline Development Group (GDG) would require for an adjunctive host-directed therapy. UNGROUNDED, though the thread lists WHO GDG requirements as a source to check.

evidence_found: (additional)**

The pragmatic cost literature suggests the cost range should include a lower bound near $5M for a very lean design. The critique's central estimate of $25–40M therefore depends on assuming TB-trial costs of several hundred dollars or more per participant.
No clear consensus exists on appropriate endpoints for HDT trials.
This supports the open question about what evidence would be needed.
caveats: I recomputed the sample sizes with the standard two-proportion formula, α=0.05 two-sided, 80% power (z-sum² = 7.849).
5.0% → 4.5% mortality:** VERIFIED. n per arm = 7.849 × (0.0475 + 0.042975) / 0.000025 ≈ 28,400, so about 56,800 in total. The critique says about 28,000 per arm and 57,000 in total.

original.thread_name: Structural — counterfactual definition of "speedup," attribution
original.title: The speedup benefit and the all-in cost come from different counterfactuals. Every coherent framing gives roughly 10–20x higher SROI.
original.hypothesis:
The BOTEC counts benefit as one year of plateau-level deaths averted. That is the value of shifting the whole pathway one year earlier, so the counterfactual is "the same pathway happens later." It then charges the full $7M pathway as cost. That is the cost of the world where the pathway never happens otherwise. The numerator comes from the "delay" world and the denominator from the "never" world. No single counterfactual yields this ratio.

I derived the ratio under each coherent framing. Let PV_B be the present value of the whole program's benefits (including p_success), and PV_C the PV of its costs.

- **Pure delay (others would fund it D years later).** Delaying the whole program by D years loses (1−e^(−rD))·PV_B in benefits. It also defers (1−e^(−rD))·PV_C in costs. The real cost of acceleration is therefore only the interest on moving ~$7M forward, about r·D·PV_C. The ratio of benefit to cost is **PV_B/PV_C, independent of D**. The $6.7M downstream spend is not a cost of the grant. It is only the time value of money pulled forward.
- **Never (no one else would run it).** Benefits are PV_B over all future years. The cost is PV_C. The ratio is again **PV_B/PV_C**.
- **Mixture with probability q of "never."** Numerator and denominator both scale by the same factor, so the ratio is again PV_B/PV_C.

The BOTEC's ratio is instead roughly (one year of plateau benefit)/(full cost), which is far smaller than PV_B/PV_C whenever benefits last many years.
original.mechanism:
PV_B/PV_C is approximately (BOTEC SROI) × (effective benefit-years in PV terms) × (a cost-discount adjustment).

- Under illustrative assumptions of r = 4% plus the model's 2% annual decline in cases, the effective benefit-years are about 1/(0.06) ≈ 17, times a delay factor of about 0.6–0.7. That gives about 10–11 benefit-years.
- Adjusting for discounted costs (÷ ~0.85) gives about 12–13x.
- Without the 2% decline and with r = 4%, it is about 18x.
- This implies a coherent SROI on the order of **30,000–55,000x versus ~3,050x**.
- The result is bounded by a finite adoption horizon, drug or regimen obsolescence, and the fact that other funders' dollars are not free.
- The ranking (coherent framing ≥ BOTEC) holds under any horizon longer than about 1.5–2 years of effective benefit.
- The number to report is the coherent ratio, not the 10–20x multiple itself. The multiple depends on horizon assumptions that I had to assume.

A separate but related issue is whose dollars count. The all-in ratio treats other funders' money as equal in value to CG's. If that money would otherwise fund TB research at similar cost-effectiveness, displacement should be charged. That would reduce the delay-branch benefit and is not captured in either framing.
suggested_evidence: Logical and algebraic argument (my own derivation). It requires no external source. It does require the CEA to confirm that the benefit really is "1 year × plateau annual deaths averted." UNGROUNDED as to whether CG has an internal rationale for the hybrid framing, for example deliberate conservatism. If CG describes the choice as deliberately conservative, the finding becomes "the framing is knowingly biased low by roughly an order of magnitude" rather than an error.

evidence_found: No external empirical evidence is needed for the core argument. I found nothing that contradicts it.
The result is highly sensitive to the benefit horizon. The Investigator notes this but then states a 30,000–55,000× headline. That headline should be treated as an upper-bound illustration only.
Real-world constraints on the horizon are visible in the statin evidence. ROSETTA found rosuvastatin 10 mg was safe but did not produce substantive benefits on culture conversion overall.
Its PET-CT analysis showed no effect on microbiological or radiological outcomes. A phase IIA atorvastatin study showed a significant reduction in sputum mycobacterial load.
Statin class and dose effects are uncertain, and p_success should be modest. The Investigator says p_success is included in PV_B, so this lowers the level but not the ratio logic.
caveats: Pure-delay algebra: VERIFIED as a derivation, with one caveat.**
If the whole program shifts by D years, benefits and costs both scale by e^(−rD). The net effect is (1−e^(−rD))·PV_B against (1−e^(−rD))·PV_C. The ratio is PV_B/PV_C, independent of D.

This is a standard result for pure time-shifts under a constant discount rate. It holds only if the benefit stream and cost stream shift by the same D. If the benefit lag is longer than the cost lag, the ratio changes.
"Never" and mixture branches: VERIFIED.** Both numerator and denominator scale by the same factor, so the ratio is PV_B/PV_C.
Numbers: VERIFIED as arithmetic, with one undocumented input.**
1/0.06 ≈ 16.7. Multiplying by 0.6–0.7 gives about 10–11.7. Dividing by 0.85 gives about 12–13.8.
With r = 4% only, 25 × 0.6–0.7 ÷ 0.85 is about 17.6–20.6, so "about 18x" holds.
The 0.6–0.7 delay factor is unexplained. It presumably reflects benefit onset after trial, WHO review and rollout. It should be stated explicitly because it drives the result.

"The BOTEC counts one year of plateau deaths averted and charges the full $7M": UNVERIFIABLE.** I do not have the CEA, so the diagnosis that the numerator and denominator come from different counterfactuals rests on the Investigator's reading.
Hybrid framing may be deliberate conservatism: UNGROUNDED, as the Investigator says.**

Displacement of other funders' money: a valid conceptual point.** The delay-branch ratio is PV_B/PV_C only if the other funders' dollars are valued at zero opportunity cost. The Investigator flags this but does not quantify it. If the displaced money would fund equally cost-effective research, the delay benefit shrinks toward zero and the 10–20× uplift would not hold.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
- Under a pure time-shift, "never", or a mixture of the two, the benefit-to-cost ratio is PV_B/PV_C. The BOTEC's "one year of benefit against full cost" is internally inconsistent if that is what the BOTEC does. That last point needs confirmation against the CEA.
- The uplift is plausibly about 10–20× under the stated horizon and discount assumptions. It depends heavily on the unexplained delay factor, the horizon, and treating other funders' dollars as free.
- Report the uplift as an illustrative range, not as "30,000–55,000×".
- Direction: the ratio rises, but displacement and horizon limits could pull it back down. Strength: large conceptually, medium once displacement is applied.

original.thread_name: Structural — counterfactual definition of "speedup," attribution
original.title: The funding landscape for a generic-statin TB program makes "never" a live branch. The speedup is a poor proxy for the grant's real counterfactual.
original.hypothesis:
Statins are off-patent and cheap. The Phase III-scale trial needed for a WHO recommendation has no commercial sponsor. The plausible funders are NIH (Johns Hopkins and related groups have published preclinical and early clinical work, which I recall but cannot cite precisely), EDCTP, Unitaid, Gates, MRC, and national agencies. Public-health funders have so far favored novel regimens, shortened regimens, and vaccines over host-directed therapies. If so, the realistic counterfactual for a CG-funded Phase IIc is not "same trial in one year" but a long, uncertain delay, or never. That is a distribution, not a point value.

If the grant is the gating event for this pathway (dose-finding precedes Phase III), the speedup has a structure the BOTEC does not model:

- With probability q, a gap of 3+ years, or never.
- With probability 1−q, a delay of 0.5–2 years.
- The expected effective speedup is q·H_eff + (1−q)·D, where H_eff is the effective horizon of benefits (about 10+ years by my Critique 1 calculation).
- Even for modest q (say 0.1–0.2), this exceeds 1 year.

original.title: Probability weighting is asymmetric between benefit and cost.
original.hypothesis: Benefits are multiplied by p_success = 0.40. If the $7M cost is a nominal sum of all stages, the denominator ignores that later-stage spend only occurs if earlier stages succeed. original.title: A 1-year speedup of trial results does not necessarily become a 1-year speedup of adoption, in either direction.
original.hypothesis:
The model assumes a pure translation of the adoption curve by one year. That holds only if the trial is the binding constraint on adoption. For a generic adjunct drug, adoption requires a WHO guideline (via a Guideline Development Group cycle), national policy updates, and procurement or training. Each step has its own lags and queue. If some steps are slack-bound (for example, WHO guideline updates occur on a roughly fixed schedule), earlier trial results may be absorbed into waiting time, giving a speedup of less than one year. The effect could be asymmetric: trial results arriving just after a guideline window close could cost a full cycle (2+ years) for a short delay. In that case the speedup is more than a year.

The speedup is therefore a random variable with a lumpy distribution. The expected value could differ from the point estimate in either direction, and 1 year may be a reasonable central value but not a defensible point value.
original.mechanism: `speedup_years` is linear in SROI. The materiality threshold is a speedup of about 0.65 years. A loss of one guideline cycle on a short delay would push the effective speedup well above 1. Slack absorption would push it below 0.65 only if the guideline pipeline were slack-bound for more than a third of the year. I cannot estimate the probabilities. Magnitude is uncertain and requires sensitivity analysis.
suggested_evidence: UNGROUNDED. The WHO guideline process for TB (Guideline Development Groups, a public call for data) is institutional, and I do not have a source on cycle lengths. The Verifier should check historical lags between pivotal trial publication and WHO guideline changes for TB regimens (for example, the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen of Study 31/A5349 and the shift to BPaLM). I believe this is a concern but cannot cite specific lags.

evidence_found: Limits of the evidence:**
These are two TB regimen cases with unusually high-profile, sponsor-supported trials. The investigator's "generic adjunct drug" may face a slower process.

The BPaLM case shows WHO acting on interim, pre-publication data. For a trial result, "available to WHO" and "published" are different dates, and the speedup definition needs to say which one is meant.
No source found quantifying lags for adjunct or host-directed therapies, or for national policy and procurement steps.
caveats: WHO guidelines come via a GDG process: VERIFIED.**
For Study 31, WHO received data from the Study 31 investigators in 2021 and convened a GDG to review the results.
WHO updates occur on a roughly fixed schedule, so earlier results are absorbed into waiting time: NOT SUPPORTED by the two TB examples.**
Study 31 was published online May 5, 2021 , and WHO's rapid communication on it was dated June 2021 (
GDG convened in 2021 after Study 31 data were received, with detailed results published 6 May 2021 ).
That is roughly one month, so the GDG was convened in response to data and not on a fixed cycle.
The consolidated guideline update followed in May 2022 .
BPaLM: GDG timing followed data availability.**
The GDG met in February–March 2022, using new evidence from the TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix trials.
TB-PRACTECAL stopped enrolling once its data safety board indicated BPaLM was superior.
The interim analysis used outcomes up to March 18, 2021.
That is about 11 months before the GDG, so most of the delay sat in data analysis and sponsor sharing, not in a WHO queue.
WHO then published its rapid communication in May 2022.
Downstream lags exist and are additive: VERIFIED for Study 31.**
CDC issued guidance on a 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen on February 25, 2022 , about 9.5 months after publication.
These sequential lags shift with the trial date and do not by themselves absorb the speedup.
Missing a guideline window costs a full cycle (2+ years): UNVERIFIED.** I found no evidence of fixed windows at WHO's TB programme. The sources suggest ad hoc GDGs, so the asymmetry may not apply.
Threshold arithmetic ("more than a third of a year" of slack): VERIFIED.** It is 1−0.65=0.35.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
- The model's one-for-one translation of the adoption curve holds only if the trial is the binding constraint at every step, and the speedup should be treated as a distribution.
- For TB specifically, two recent regimens show WHO's GDG responding within about one to two months of data being shared. That favours a speedup close to 1 year at the WHO stage and weakens the "fixed guideline cycle" mechanism and the asymmetric "lost cycle" upside.
- The remaining uncertainty lies in national adoption and procurement lags, plus the unspecified definition of the trial-result date. The post-WHO lags are untested here.
- **Strength: low-to-medium. Direction: uncertain (slightly toward "≈1 year or modestly less").** The lumpy-cycle claim is UNGROUNDED for TB. I recommend a sensitivity band on speedup_years instead of a point value.

original.title: Post-TB lung disease morbidity is likely the largest unvalued channel (~50–60k central, wide range)
original.hypothesis: The trial's strongest signal was reduced lung damage, and the BOTEC gives it zero value. Post-TB lung disease (airflow obstruction, restrictive impairment, bronchiectasis, and chronic breathlessness) affects a large share of survivors for decades. Even a modest proportional reduction in that burden, applied to 3.3M patients, is not trivial relative to a 535k base.
original.mechanism:
This adds a new term: patients × baseline post-TB morbidity DALYs × relative reduction × probability weight.
- Baseline per patient (inference): about 30% have clinically meaningful impairment. Average disability weight is ~0.1–0.2 (GBD chronic respiratory states, which I'd verify) over ~15–25 years. That gives ~2.5 DALYs per affected patient, or ~0.75 DALYs per treated patient. The pool is then 3.3M × 0.75 ≈ 2.5M DALYs per adoption-year.
- Reduction attributable to the intervention: 5% central. This is deliberately lower than the trial's lung-damage signal, to allow for surrogate attenuation. The range is 2–15%.
- Pre-p: 2.5M × 0.05 ≈ 124k.
- Probability weight: ~0.45. This is p_success = 0.4, plus a small contribution from the branch where the mortality endpoint fails but the lung benefit is real and still leads to adoption (see Critique 4).
- Result: ~55k central. The range is ~10k (2% reduction, lower baseline) to ~300k (15% reduction, ~1.5 DALYs per patient baseline).
- By itself this is below the 134k threshold. It reaches the threshold only in the upper half of the range.

Under CG's no-discounting convention these decades-long DALYs count in full. That inflates this channel relative to a discounted calculation, so it is partly an artifact of the convention. I would report both versions.
suggested_evidence: Menzies et al. 2021 (Lancet Glob Health, systematic review and meta-analysis of lifetime TB burden) reportedly attributes a substantial share of lifetime DALYs per incident case to post-TB sequelae. I believe the share is large but cannot confirm the exact proportion. The Verifier should check it, since it anchors my baseline (0.75 DALYs per patient).

The International Post-TB Symposium consensus and Allwood et al. document the high prevalence of post-TB lung disease. The prevalence and disability-weight inputs above are my own inference from that literature, not quoted values.

The link between reduced early lung damage and long-term function is not established in an RCT with long follow-up. That is UNGROUNDED for the specific statin effect size, and the 5% figure is my assumption.

The convention flag is correct. Menzies shows a large share of DALYs accrue after 15 or more years, so discounting would cut this channel materially.

Reviews put respiratory impairment among TB survivors at 15–60%.
The "~30% with meaningful impairment" input sits inside that range.
Baseline of 0.75 DALYs per patient: **PLAUSIBLE but probably low.**

original.title: Post-treatment excess mortality (~40–50k central) and a related sign-reversing adjustment
original.hypothesis: TB survivors have a substantially elevated long-term all-cause mortality rate compared with matched controls. Part of that is respiratory and plausibly linked to residual lung damage. A lung-sparing adjunct could avert some of these deaths, in addition to the on-treatment deaths CG values. There is also a counterweight. CG's DALYs per on-treatment death averted presumably assume near-normal remaining life expectancy, but the patients rescued from death are those with advanced disease, who are likely to have a worse post-TB prognosis.
original.mechanism:
There are two opposite-signed adjustments.

**(a) Upside, excess-death channel** (inference-based arithmetic):
- Cumulative excess mortality over ~10 years: ~10% of survivors. Romanowski 2019 reports elevated post-treatment mortality, but the specific values here are my illustrative assumption.
- Share attributable to lung and respiratory sequelae: ~40%. This is UNGROUNDED.
- Reduction attributable to the intervention: 5%.
- Deaths averted: 0.10 × 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.002 per patient.
- DALYs per death averted at the typical age of death: ~15.
- Result: 0.03 DALYs per patient × 3.3M ≈ 100k pre-p, or ~45k after weighting.
- The statin's own cardiovascular benefit over a ~6-month course is negligible. I'd treat it as zero.

**(b) Downside, life-expectancy adjustment:**
- If on-treatment deaths averted are valued at standard life expectancy, the benefit is overstated by roughly 5–10%. This applies to a subpopulation with higher baseline mortality (HIV, malnutrition, advanced disease).
- Applied to 535k, that is about −25k to −55k.
- The two adjustments could nearly cancel. A net-zero effect is possible.
suggested_evidence: Romanowski et al. 2019 (Lancet Infect Dis) is the primary source for elevated post-treatment mortality. I recall the pooled all-cause mortality being a multiple of the general population's, but I have not confirmed the number.
The respiratory attribution share and the "advanced disease lowers residual life expectancy" argument are my own inference. UNGROUNDED pending verification.

evidence_found: Menzies's post-TB DALYs include post-TB mortality, so this channel overlaps with Critique 1 if both are added.
Mortality is elevated in the Cerqueira-Silva cohort even in treated patients, supporting the existence of the excess-death pool but not the 40% lung share or the 5% effect.
The net effect is unsigned. The Investigator's own conclusion that the two adjustments may cancel is reasonable.
caveats: Elevated post-treatment mortality: **VERIFIED.** A large 2025 Brazilian cohort also found an elevated natural-cause mortality risk in the treated cohort (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.55–2.03).
Risk ratios were raised for respiratory deaths, among other causes.
Respiratory disease as a major driver of excess deaths: **PARTIALLY VERIFIED.** One review states that respiratory diseases remain the leading cause of excess deaths in people who recover from TB.
The 40% attributable share is not directly sourced. For comparison, Romanowski attributed 20% (95% CI 15–26) of the excess to cardiovascular disease ( per the Basham et al. discussion
). A respiratory share of 40% is therefore plausible but **UNGROUNDED**.

5% intervention effect: **UNGROUNDED.**

original.title: Transmission benefit is small, with a bounded calculation (~10–30k central)
original.hypothesis: Faster culture conversion could shorten infectiousness. Because most transmission occurs before diagnosis, and infectiousness falls quickly after effective therapy starts, the incremental effect is small. But the benefit chains through to secondary cases, so a tiny fractional change is not negligible.
original.mechanism:
- Direct secondary disease cases per index case: ~0.3–1 (inference).
- Share of an index case's lifetime transmission occurring after treatment start: ~1–5% (inference, UNGROUNDED).
- Fractional reduction in that post-start transmission from a faster conversion: ~10–20%.
- Net transmission reduction: ~0.1–1%, with 0.3% as central.
- DALYs per secondary case (including its mortality and morbidity): ~10.
- Calculation: 3.3M × 0.5 secondary cases × 0.003 × 10 ≈ 50k pre-p, or ~20k after weighting.
- The range is ~3k to ~150k, with a heavy upper tail.
- Two further adjustments push the estimate down:
  - Sputum culture conversion at 8 weeks does not map one-to-one to infectiousness reduction.
  - Fewer secondary cases are averted if the incidence trend and treated-share assumptions are already near saturation.
suggested_evidence: The literature on rapid infectiousness decline after starting effective therapy and on pre-diagnosis transmission supports the logic. I cannot name specific studies with confidence. UNGROUNDED, and the Verifier should find the most relevant modelling studies.
All numerical inputs are my own inference.

evidence_found: Modelling sources that fit the Investigator's logic:
The shorter-regimen model (PMC4015982).
Dowdy-type pre-diagnosis transmission analyses (PMC9907102).
The infectiousness and effective-treatment review (PMC12054730).
Shorter-regimen modelling treats on-treatment infectiousness as short-lived. This supports the idea that conversion speed after week 2 matters little.
Counterweight to the Investigator's logic: a lung-sparing adjunct does not shorten diagnostic delay, which is the dominant transmission window. This reinforces the small-effect conclusion.
caveats: Most transmission occurs before diagnosis and treatment start: **VERIFIED.** A review on infectiousness and treatment effect says most TB transmission occurs before diagnosis and effective treatment initiation.
A Bayesian modelling study finds a disproportionate share of future transmission arises from undiagnosed smear-positive subclinical TB.
Infectiousness falls quickly after effective therapy starts: **VERIFIED, with caveats.**
A population model of shorter regimens assumes bacillary burden drops rapidly and patients are non-infectious after the first two weeks.
The same review reports that
30–40% of patients who produce cough aerosols rapidly become nonculturable after treatment initiation.
Human-to-guinea-pig experiments show a rapid effect of effective treatment on transmission.
However, the exact duration of infectiousness after treatment initiation remains uncertain and likely varies between individuals.
A 1–5% post-start transmission share is directionally supported but not directly measured.
Culture conversion at 8 weeks does not map one-to-one to infectiousness: **PLAUSIBLE.** Conversion at 8 weeks is a phase 2b efficacy endpoint ( usually measured at 2 months
). Infectiousness collapses much earlier than culture conversion, so the Investigator's discount is warranted.
ROSETTA, a statin trial, found no benefit on culture conversion.
Another trial using rosuvastatin did not affect sputum culture conversion.
An atorvastatin phase IIA study did show a significant reduction in sputum mycobacterial load.
The premise of faster conversion is therefore contested across trials.
Secondary cases per index case of 0.3–1: **UNVERIFIABLE** here. It is plausible for high-burden settings but not sourced.
10 DALYs per secondary case: **PLAUSIBLE.** Menzies gives an average of 12.1 DALYs per incident case.
Arithmetic: **VERIFIED.** 3.3M × 0.5 × 0.003 × 10 ≈ 49.5k; × 0.4 ≈ 20k. The net 0.1–1% follows from 1–5% × 10–20%. The 3k–150k range is unverified.
critique.revised_hypothesis: Most transmission occurs before diagnosis, and infectiousness falls within days to weeks of effective treatment. Any transmission benefit from faster culture conversion is therefore small. This is supported by the transmission and modelling literature above. The numerical inputs (post-start transmission share of 1–5%, 10–20% reduction, 0.5 secondary cases) are unsourced and should be flagged **UNGROUNDED**. The central estimate of ~20k is a bounded order-of-magnitude figure, with real downside if the statin has no culture-conversion effect (ROSETTA found none). Consider lowering the central estimate toward ~10k or below, and widening the low end toward zero. Strength: low. This is a minor channel, and the thread label ("post-TB lung disease") does not match its content.

original.thread_name: Unvalued benefits — post-TB lung disease, long-term post-treatment
original.title: The "lung benefit without mortality benefit" scenario is structurally less valuable than a simple p_success weighting implies
original.hypothesis:
The thread's framing suggests the unvalued channels might make the estimate "robust even if the on-treatment mortality effect is small." That holds only if a surrogate-only result still leads to adoption at similar scale. The Phase III endpoint, and what WHO guideline bodies require, determines this.
- If the trial's primary endpoint is something like unfavorable outcome or relapse rather than lung function, a lung-only benefit would not obviously earn a recommendation.
- Adoption would also require willingness to pay for an additional drug for 3.3M patients.
- This gives an adoption probability in the "mortality fails, lung holds" branch well below the 60% uptake CG assumes. I'd guess ≤10–20%, but this is UNGROUNDED.
original.mechanism:
This is a correction to how Critiques 1–3 are weighted, not a separate value term.
- Simple weighting: p_success × full uptake. If I naively applied the same 60% uptake in the lung-only branch, the lung channel would be up to ~2× higher (a probability of roughly 0.4 + 0.6 × P(lung holds | mortality fails) instead of 0.45).
- Realistic weighting, with P(lung holds | mortality fails) at 0.3–0.5 and conditional adoption of 10–20%, adds only ~0.02–0.06 to the 0.4 base. That supports the ~0.45 figure I used.
- Net effect: the lung channel is closer to 1× than 2× its p_success-weighted value, which limits the upside. Anyone who weights it by a "surrogate holds" probability alone without discounting for adoption will overstate it.
suggested_evidence: Logical and structural argument about regulatory and guideline pathways. I cannot identify a specific source for this trial's registered endpoints. UNGROUNDED.
The Verifier should check the Phase IIc and planned Phase III endpoints, and how WHO guideline development weighs lung-function surrogates.

evidence_found: Lung function is a recognized preliminary-efficacy outcome in adjunctive host-directed therapy trials. A Phase 2 RCT of CC-11050 and everolimus suggests they might enhance recovery of FEV1, a measure of lung function and predictor of all-cause mortality . This supports P(lung holds) being non-trivial. It says nothing about whether FEV1 alone would drive a WHO recommendation.
I found no evidence on how WHO guideline groups weigh lung-function surrogates.
caveats: Adoption in the lung-only branch is ≤10–20%:** UNVERIFIABLE. It is a judgment call, and no source on WHO guideline handling of lung-function surrogates turned up.
Realistic weighting adds ~0.02–0.06 to the 0.4 base:** VERIFIED as arithmetic. 0.6 × (0.3–0.5) × (0.1–0.2) = 0.018–0.06, so the total is about 0.42–0.46.
Naive weighting gives "up to ~2×":** PARTIALLY VERIFIED. At the stated inputs, 0.4 + 0.6 × (0.3–0.5) = 0.58–0.70, which is about 1.45–1.75× the base. "Up to ~2×" is a mild overstatement.
Conflation of terms:** MISLEADING WORDING. The text calls 0.6 the "60% uptake". In the formula, 0.6 is P(mortality fails), which is 1 − 0.4. These are different parameters.

Direction label:** FLAG. The argument says the lung channel is worth *less* than a naive weighting implies. That is a correction toward ~1×, not an increase. "Increases" only makes sense relative to the 0.4 base, and the size is negligible (+0.02–0.06).
critique.revised_hypothesis:
Treat this as a structural caveat, not a quantified adjustment. If the trial's registered endpoint is not lung function, a lung-only result probably earns a lower adoption probability than the main-case uptake. The 0.45 figure is arithmetically consistent with the Investigator's inputs. The 10–20% conditional adoption is UNGROUNDED. The direction should read "neutral to slightly decreases relative to a naive weighting". Magnitude is small, not medium.

original.thread_name: Implementation — trial execution, guideline adoption pathway,
original.title: 60% steady-state uptake has no precedent among comparable TB program additions
original.hypothesis: CG's 60% is justified as "generic and cheap." Cost is only one of several determinants of uptake in TB programs. Comparable additions have often taken many years to reach even moderate coverage, and some stall below 50%. These include Xpert MTB/RIF (WHO endorsement 2010), the 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen (WHO 2022), and adjunctive dexamethasone for TB meningitis (evidence 2004, widely recommended afterward). Adjunctive pyridoxine with isoniazid has also been recommended for years but is inconsistently supplied. An adjunct with no direct patient-visible benefit (it does not shorten treatment) and a separate pill is, if anything, a harder sell than diagnostics or regimens that simplify care. 60% is therefore plausibly an upper-bound or optimistic-case value, not a central one.
original.mechanism: adult_uptake enters roughly linearly. Reducing the long-run ceiling to 0.30–0.40 (the materiality line is 0.39) cuts SROI by 33–50%. Ramp shape matters little for a one-year speedup over an infinite horizon, because shifting any ramp by one year gains about (ceiling × one year of cases). So the ceiling matters much more than the ramp. The ramp only matters through a finite horizon, incidence decline and discounting (Thread 3).
suggested_evidence: Logical argument plus my recollection of precedents. I believe WHO Global TB Reports show that well over a decade after endorsement, Xpert/WRD was still the initial test for well under 100% of notified cases (roughly 40–50% in recent reports), but I cannot give an exact figure or citation, so this is UNGROUNDED as to numbers. I believe the dexamethasone-for-TBM and pyridoxine examples are real, but I cannot cite specific coverage data. Type of evidence: inference from precedents, not a direct study. The Verifier should pull WHO Global TB Report WRD-testing percentages by year and the HPMZ rollout data (GDF orders, number of countries adopting).

evidence_found: WRD coverage rose in 24 African countries from 37% in 2018 to 58% in 2023 . That is about 4 percentage points per year, a useful ramp-rate benchmark.
WHO's Guideline Development Group framed the 4-month regimen as an option whose uptake would grow
"in future as uptake of this regimen improves" . This shows WHO itself anticipated gradual uptake.
caveats: "Comparable additions often take many years to reach moderate coverage":** VERIFIED for WRD (14 years to 54%) and 4HPMZ.
"Some stall below 50%":** PARTIALLY VERIFIED. 4HPMZ is well below 50%. WRD is at 54%, not below 50%.

The 4HPMZ analogy is imperfect.** Its slow uptake is driven mainly by rifapentine supply, adverse events and a high pill burden. A cheap generic adjunct isn't supply-constrained in the same way. The Investigator's claim that an adjunct is a "harder sell" than regimens that simplify care is a reasonable inference, but it is inference.
WRD is also an imperfect analog.** It needs instruments, cartridges and labs. A generic pill avoids that infrastructure barrier.

"60% has no precedent":** FALSE as worded. The WRD benchmark (54% after 14 years, with many countries above 80%) suggests 60% is reachable but optimistic on a short horizon. "Plausibly an upper-bound or optimistic-case value" is defensible. "No precedent" is not.
Arithmetic:** VERIFIED. Cutting the ceiling from 60% to 40% or 30% reduces SROI by 33% or 50% under linear scaling. The "materiality line is 0.39" is internal to the model and unverifiable here.
"Ceiling matters more than ramp":** PLAUSIBLE. It is logically sound for an undiscounted infinite horizon. The Investigator acknowledges the caveats (finite horizon, incidence decline, discounting).
critique.revised_hypothesis: CG's 60% steady-state uptake looks optimistic relative to TB program precedent. The strongest verified analogs are WRD at 54% global coverage after ~14 years (heavily skewed by country) and 4HPMZ with slow, supply- and tolerability-limited uptake. Neither is a clean analog for a cheap generic adjunct. Reducing the ceiling to 0.30–0.40 cuts SROI by about 33–50% under linear scaling. The 60% figure is a plausible optimistic or upper-central case, not an impossible one. The dexamethasone and pyridoxine examples should be dropped or flagged as UNVERIFIED. Direction is "decreases". Magnitude is medium to large, but the evidence supports the ceiling being uncertain rather than demonstrably too high. I would rate the critique's strength as moderate. Pulling country-level adoption data for comparable adjuncts would strengthen it.

original.title: A Phase III cannot be powered on mortality, so the WHO GDG would be recommending on surrogate or composite endpoints
original.hypothesis: CG's value is entirely mortality-based. If the modeled relative reduction (~10%) refers to mortality in DS-TB, a Phase III cannot feasibly detect it. On-treatment mortality in DS-TB is perhaps 3–6% in many settings, though higher with HIV or in severe disease. Detecting a 10% relative reduction from a 5% baseline (absolute 0.5 pp; alpha 0.05, power 80%) needs roughly 2 × (2.8)² × 0.0475 / 0.005² ≈ 30,000 per arm. That is my own calculation and rests on the assumed baseline. The realistic Phase III will therefore use relapse-free cure, unfavorable outcome, culture conversion or lung function. The GDG (GRADE) would then rate certainty down for indirectness on the mortality benefit. A recommendation could be delayed, made conditional, or made only for subgroups (e.g., high-risk, HIV-negative, severe disease). The adoption probability and uptake given a "positive" trial are therefore lower than CG's "if it works → 60%."
original.mechanism: This lowers adult_uptake (conditional recommendations produce lower uptake). It may also lengthen years_to_adoption if the GDG requests additional evidence. It also means the mortality effect that drives all benefits is never directly verified, which raises the variance of the realized relative_reduction (Thread 1). The direction is downward on uptake. Quantification is uncertain: a conditional recommendation limited to a subgroup (e.g., a third of patients) would cut effective uptake by about half or more, but that scenario is speculative.
suggested_evidence: Logical and statistical argument (sample size calculation above, which depends on the 5% and 10% inputs). On GRADE, I believe indirectness from surrogate outcomes is a standard downgrading criterion in the WHO handbook for guideline development, but the Verifier should check the handbook text. The baseline mortality figure is UNGROUNDED and needs a source (WHO Global TB Report treatment-outcome data).

evidence_found: The GRADE downgrade applies specifically to the mortality outcome. If the Phase III reports unfavorable outcome, which includes death, WHO TB guidelines have historically treated treatment outcomes as critical outcomes. A recommendation therefore need not stall. It would simply carry a "mortality benefit not directly shown" caveat. This weakens the "delay" pathway and leaves the "modeled benefit is unverified" pathway intact.
The sample-size problem is worse for a trial restricted to a high-risk subgroup, because the trial then enrolls fewer patients.
caveats: Sample size of about 30,000 per arm: VERIFIED (arithmetic).**
The Investigator's formula gives about 29,800.
The standard two-proportion formula (5% vs 4.5%, alpha 0.05 two-sided, 80% power) gives about 28,400 per arm.
Both round to roughly 30,000, so the conclusion holds. It depends entirely on the 5% baseline and 10% relative reduction.
GRADE downgrades for indirectness when a surrogate stands in for a patient-important outcome: VERIFIED.**
GRADE guidance says that when a surrogate is used, authors should rate down the quality of evidence for indirectness of outcome.
WHO's own SAGE guidance lists surrogate end-points as an example of indirectness.

WHO guidelines that follow the WHO handbook define indirectness as including differences in populations, interventions, comparisons or outcomes of interest between the research and the target context.
WHO's DR-TB guidelines also list indirectness among the criteria for rating certainty down.
I could not retrieve the handbook text itself. The claim is supported through WHO documents that apply it.
On-treatment DS-TB mortality of about 3–6%: UNVERIFIABLE in this session.**
My search for WHO Global TB Report treatment-outcome data failed.
From background knowledge the range is plausible, but I have no citation.
It still needs sourcing.
The realistic Phase III will use culture conversion, relapse-free cure, unfavorable outcome or lung function: PLAUSIBLE.**
Existing statin and host-directed-therapy trials use surrogate endpoints.

A phase 2 host-directed-therapy trial used recovery of FEV1.
Lower uptake, a delayed or conditional recommendation, or subgroup-only recommendations: PLAUSIBLE but UNGROUNDED.**

A Phase III powered on mortality is infeasible. About 28,000–30,000 per arm would be needed at a 5% baseline and 10% relative reduction, and both inputs are assumptions. The trial will likely use a surrogate or composite endpoint. GRADE and WHO methods support downgrading the mortality evidence for indirectness. Statins carry label warnings for active liver disease and transaminase elevation, and are historically avoided in pregnancy. Clinicians managing a TB patient with rising ALT will plausibly not want an additional agent that confounds attribution of DILI, and may stop it. Programs would likely require baseline and follow-up LFTs, which many NTP settings do not routinely perform for DS-TB. Also relevant are drug–drug interactions (rifampicin induction of CYP3A4; some protease-inhibitor-based ART raises atorvastatin exposure, while efavirenz lowers it) and pill-burden aversion. FDC regimens are valued precisely because they avoid extra pills.

In addition, the shift toward the 4-month rifapentine-containing regimen (HPMZ) matters because rifapentine is generally considered a strong CYP3A4 inducer, comparable to or stronger than rifampicin in some dosing contexts. Dose-finding in a Phase IIc is performed on one regimen (presumably rifampicin-based HRZE), so the dose selected may not carry over.

The "70% adherence" figure is from the thread's materiality framing, not an empirical estimate.

AUC at 50% or less in five of ten subjects.
The statin choice therefore changes the size of this problem.

I found no direct study.

I did not search for this.
It is widely reported in general populations, but the transfer to a 6-month TB course is an assumption.
The Investigator admits having no TB-specific source.

HPMZ is "currently small but growing": UNVERIFIED.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
Two separate concerns remain:
1. **Adherence and delivered dose.** Real-world adherence to an out-of-FDC adjunct plausibly falls below trial adherence. Illustratively, 70% adherence would cut effective uptake from 0.60 to 0.42. The 70% figure is a framing assumption, not data, and the TB-specific adherence evidence is UNGROUNDED. This part keeps medium strength.
2. **Rifamycin interaction and dose transfer.** Rifamycins substantially lower atorvastatin exposure. Daily rifapentine induces CYP3A4 at roughly 85–100% of rifampicin's level. The claim that rifapentine is "stronger" than rifampicin should be dropped, and the interaction should not be presented as specifically worse in HPMZ. The rifapentine magnitude is UNGROUNDED. Reduce this part to **low** strength.

original.title: Zero modeled lag between Phase III completion and adoption, and a speedup that assumes trial timing is the binding constraint

National adoption and procurement then took additional years. Separately, the 8-year timeline itself is exposed to execution risk. TB trials, particularly those run at multiple high-burden sites with a relapse endpoint requiring 12–24 months of follow-up, routinely slip. A generic drug also has no commercial sponsor, so Phase III funding could be a gating constraint, not the Phase IIc result. If so, a 1-year acceleration of the Phase IIc does not translate one-for-one into a 1-year earlier adoption.

I note that lumpy decision cycles by themselves do not lower the expected speedup (if the timing is uniformly random, the expected shift equals the trial shift), so the case for a lower speedup rests on the trial not being the binding constraint, not on lumpiness.

For Xpert, WHO endorsement was in 2010, and implementation took many years afterward (Albert et al., Cazabon et al. are the sources the thread names; I have not confirmed their specific findings). The Phase III funding-gap argument is a logical inference. Phase IIc registry timelines are not something I can cite.

original.thread_name: Who dies and how many healthy years are lost —
original.title: Survivors' excess mortality and comorbidity shrink the 27 DALYs per death
original.hypothesis: CG describes 27 as the "remaining healthy life expectancy" of a person who dies of TB. A person whose death is averted is not an average member of the population. TB patients carry high rates of smoking, alcohol use, diabetes, undernutrition, HIV and post-TB lung damage. Their expected remaining life after cure is therefore shorter than a general-population life table implies. If 27 comes from general-population or GBD-style life tables, it overstates the years gained per death averted.
original.mechanism:
dalys_per_death falls. Illustrative calculation (my own inference, not from a source):
- Under Gompertz mortality, multiplying the hazard by a factor k is roughly equivalent to ageing by ln(k)/b years. For b ≈ 0.09–0.10 per year and an SMR of about 3, that is ln(3)/0.09 ≈ 11–12 years of effective ageing.
- For a patient aged about 40, remaining life expectancy in an LMIC life table is roughly low-to-mid 30s. For an effective age of about 52 it is mid-20s.
- That is a 20–30% reduction in remaining life expectancy. 27 would fall to roughly 19–22, which is near or below the 17.7 threshold once combined with any other downward adjustment.
- The shift is partly offset if 27 is already a healthy-life measure built from a TB-specific population. It is amplified if CG took general-population HALE and then applied it unadjusted.
suggested_evidence: Romanowski et al. 2019 (Lancet Infect Dis), a systematic review of long-term all-cause mortality after TB treatment. I recall a pooled SMR of roughly 3–4 versus general populations, but the exact figure needs verification.
Gompertz scaling is a standard demographic approximation.
The SMR is partly confounded by shared risk factors. That is exactly why the counterfactual years of an averted-death patient are lower than the population average.
I cannot identify a source for how CG derived 27.

evidence_found: No source for how "27" was derived. Without it, whether the proposed adjustment applies cannot be settled.
The direction (downward) is well supported by the literature. The magnitude (20–30%) rests on assumptions that cannot be verified here.
caveats: TB patients carry high rates of smoking, alcohol use, diabetes, undernutrition and HIV: VERIFIED.** A Lancet seminar says progression to disease is higher in people with undernourishment, immunosuppression, or who smoke, drink alcohol, or have diabetes.
A Georgia, USA cohort found that
HIV co-infection, excess alcohol use, diabetes and end-stage renal disease were associated with post-treatment death.

Post-TB lung damage drives excess mortality: VERIFIED.** A Lancet Global Health review states that respiratory diseases remain the leading cause of excess deaths in people who recover from TB, with mortality three to six times that of local peers.

Gompertz arithmetic: VERIFIED.** ln(3) ≈ 1.10. Dividing by 0.09–0.10 gives about 11–12 years of effective ageing, as stated. Whether b ≈ 0.09–0.10 applies to LMIC adult mortality was not checked. It is roughly standard for adult mortality.
Remaining life expectancy of about 30–35 years at age 40 and mid-20s at age 52 in LMICs: PLAUSIBLE.** I did not look up life tables. The 20–30% reduction follows from those inputs.
Result: 27 falls to about 19–22: CONDITIONAL.** This is only valid if 27 was derived from general-population life tables. That was not established.
"Near or below the 17.7 threshold": UNVERIFIABLE.** This refers to the source model.
**Weaknesses in the mechanism (my additions)**

1. **SMR heterogeneity.** The Georgia cohort found a pooled SMR of 0.89 (95% CI 0.73–1.05) , well below the Romanowski pooled estimate. It was a US cohort, but it shows SMR varies widely by setting. Romanowski's pooled value may not transfer to the countries where the HPMZ regimen would be used. A single hazard multiplier applied across all ages is also a simplification, since the commentary says excess mortality is notable among younger adults.
2. **Double-counting.** Part of the excess mortality is caused by TB sequelae, which the model may already treat elsewhere. A lifetime-burden study estimated
12.1 DALYs per incident TB case, of which 5.8 were post-TB.
If 27 is already a healthy-life figure from a TB-specific population, the adjustment would partly double-count. The Investigator acknowledged this.

3. **Averted-death patients are not the same population as treated survivors.** The Romanowski cohort was treated and survived. Patients whose deaths a shorter regimen averts are likely sicker at presentation, which supports the Investigator's direction. But it also means that applying a survivor SMR is an approximation.
critique.revised_hypothesis: TB survivors have about three times the mortality of local populations (Romanowski 2019, pooled 2.91, 95% CI 2.21–3.84). Patients whose death is averted are not average members of the population, so a general-population life table likely overstates their remaining healthy years. A simple Gompertz scaling gives an effective ageing of about 11–12 years and a 20–30% reduction in remaining life expectancy at age 40. This is the Investigator's own illustration and was not sourced. The magnitude depends on whether "27" came from a general-population table, which is unknown, and on whether the SMR transfers to the relevant countries and ages. Caveats: SMR varies by setting, and TB-specific life tables may already include much of the effect. **Direction: decreases (well supported). Magnitude: medium-to-large, conditional on the derivation of 27.** The SMR is real and the mechanism is sound. The exact size of the effect is UNGROUNDED until the derivation of 27 is checked.

baseline_mortality rises.
