original.title: The TB-specific reference classes (host-directed therapy, adjunctives, regimen-shortening) have a much worse record than 40%
original.hypothesis:
The relevant class is not "drugs" but "TB host-directed or adjunctive therapies, and TB treatment-shortening strategies promoted on animal or early-phase surrogate data". To my knowledge this class has a poor Phase III record.
- **Vitamin D.** Trials in Guinea-Bissau (Wejse et al., 2009) and London (Martineau et al., 2011) showed no mortality or overall culture-conversion benefit. I am fairly confident of this but have not checked details.
- **Fluoroquinolone 4-month regimens.** REMoxTB, OFLOTUB and RIFAQUIN failed non-inferiority in Phase III despite encouraging mouse and Phase II (culture-conversion) data. This is the closest analogue to "promising preclinical plus Phase II surrogate → Phase III".
- **Dexamethasone in HIV-associated TB meningitis.** The ACT HIV trial (2023) was, as I recall, null on survival. This is a case where an adjunctive anti-inflammatory looked effective in an earlier trial population and did not generalize.
- **Corticosteroids.** These are the counter-example: benefit in TB meningitis (Thwaites 2004) and pericarditis, and they were adopted. They are the one clear success of the class.
- **Other HDTs.** Statins, metformin and others have mostly mouse and observational support. To my knowledge no HDT is WHO-recommended for drug-sensitive pulmonary TB. Reviews such as Wallis & Hafner and Kolloli & Subbian describe a pipeline that is mostly preclinical or small Phase II.
- **Statin preclinical data.** Mouse data for pravastatin (Parihar and colleagues, Karakousis group) are promising. Observational human data (statin use and lower TB risk) are subject to healthy-user bias.

A success rate for this class of well under 40% from Phase II onward looks plausible, perhaps 10–20%. However, Study 31/A5349 (rifapentine-moxifloxacin 4-month regimen) succeeded and was adopted, so the class is not zero.

original.hypothesis:
CG's p_success is defined as "Phase II and III both succeed", and the benefit is a 10% relative mortality reduction. A Phase III TB trial cannot realistically be powered to show a 10% relative mortality reduction.

A power calculation with reasoning shown (my own arithmetic):
- Assume baseline trial-population mortality of about 4% (programmatic mortality in DS-TB is of similar order, maybe 4–6%).
- A 10% relative reduction is 0.4 percentage points (4.0% → 3.6%).
- Using n ≈ (1.96 + 0.84)² × [p₁q₁ + p₂q₂] / d², n ≈ 7.84 × 0.0731 / (0.004)² ≈ 36,000 per arm, about 70,000 in total.
- Even at 6% baseline mortality, this is still tens of thousands per arm.

Standard TB Phase III trials enroll hundreds to a few thousand and use composite "unfavorable outcome", relapse or culture-conversion endpoints. So "Phase III success" will almost certainly be declared on a surrogate or composite endpoint. The 10% mortality figure is then an extrapolation never directly tested. P(trials succeed) overstates P(adopted AND mortality benefit ≥ 10%). The mortality benefit conditional on surrogate success is uncertain and could be much smaller.
original.mechanism: The model effectively computes p_success × uptake × 10% × deaths. The coherent quantity is P(trials succeed on surrogate) × P(adopted | success) × E[mortality reduction | surrogate success, adoption]. If E[RR | surrogate success] is 5–7% rather than 10%, benefit falls 30–50%, compounding with any p_success revision. The magnitude depends on the surrogate-to-mortality relationship, which is uncertain, so it needs a sensitivity analysis. Also note that if success needs a 10% mortality effect to be real, the true probability is lower still. Unless the success definition is aligned with the 10%, the two parameters cannot both be right.
suggested_evidence: Logical and arithmetic argument, based on standard sample-size mathematics. The baseline mortality is an assumption, so the Verifier should check typical DS-TB trial mortality rates and the primary endpoints of recent Phase III trials such as Study 31, REMoxTB and TRUNCATE-TB. The surrogate-to-mortality relationship for TB adjuncts is UNGROUNDED here.

This is not strictly a probability of efficacy, and "success" at this stage may only mean "a tolerable dose with acceptable exposure was found". Industry Phase II rates of ~29% reflect proof-of-efficacy trials. A dose-finding IIc therefore does not de-risk Phase III the way a proof-of-concept Phase II would, and it may even produce an optimistic dose or a surrogate signal that Phase III later fails to confirm. REMoxTB-type experience, where Phase II culture-conversion signals did not translate, is relevant here (see Critique 2).

Implication: the 40% cannot be sanity-checked against Phase II→approval statistics without first defining the IIc endpoint. If IIc is easy and Phase III is the real hurdle, the realistic product is P(IIc) ≈ 0.7 × P(III | weak signal) ≈ 0.3 ≈ 0.21 (illustrative inference), again at or below the break-even.
original.mechanism: The same linear effect on p_success as in Critique 1, but with a different decomposition: the Phase III failure rate becomes the focus and the Phase IIc contributes little. This also affects the joint distribution of p_success and relative_reduction. A weak gate lets through a dose that may be too low for efficacy, which correlates a lower effect size with Phase III failure. If the true effect is below 10%, Phase III is also less likely to succeed. So modelling p_success and RR as independent point values can mislead. The expected value of the product E[p × RR] is not p × E[RR] when both depend on the true effect. The direction is ambiguous. Conditional on Phase III success, winner's curse suggests the realized effect on the endpoint is smaller than the 10% planning value. Conversely, successful trials select for larger true effects. A simple scenario analysis with a prior over true effect sizes would show which dominates.
suggested_evidence: Logical and theoretical argument, plus general knowledge about Phase IIc design. Direct evidence on how this specific Phase IIc defines success is UNGROUNDED here. The Verifier should check the trial protocol and the CG grant rationale.

evidence_found: Phase 2 HDT trials in TB often define success by safety and surrogates. The four-HDT Phase 2 trial in South Africa (
200 patients
) assessed safety and preliminary efficacy.
Its efficacy signal was FEV₁ recovery, a predictor of long-term all-cause mortality.
This supports the "weak gate" idea for HDT-type adjuncts in general. It does not show how this specific IIc defines success.
More data are needed before any endpoint can be used as a surrogate in a confirmatory Phase III trial.
That fits the concern that Phase II signals transmit little information.
caveats: REMoxTB: early culture-conversion signals did not translate to Phase III: VERIFIED.**
Earlier time to culture conversion failed to predict successful 4-month fluoroquinolone regimens and had limited use as a surrogate in REMoxTB.
A REMoxTB reanalysis found faster culture conversion with the moxifloxacin regimens, even though the smear-conversion analysis showed no treatment difference.
Culture conversion has only a limited role in deciding which regimens advance to Phase III.
"See Critique 2": WRONG REFERENCE.** REMoxTB is not discussed in Critique 2, only in Critique 1's suggested evidence.
Phase IIc is mainly dose-finding or PK/safety, as the "exclusion list implies": UNVERIFIABLE, and RISKY.**
In the TB field, Phase IIb trials usually use culture-conversion endpoints:
Phase IIb trials continue to use culture-conversion primary endpoints as the best available marker.
From general knowledge, "Phase IIc" in TB usually means a larger or longer proof-of-efficacy trial with clinical-outcome endpoints. I did not confirm this by search.
If so, the critique's premise that P(IIc) is 0.6–0.8 and uninformative may be wrong. The protocol or grant rationale needs checking, which the Investigator also recommended.

Industry Phase II success of about 29%: PLAUSIBLE, NOT VERIFIED HERE.** The figure matches my recollection of Phase II→III transition rates in industry benchmarking. It is a transition rate, not Phase II→approval, so the critique's phrase "Phase II→approval statistics" mixes two measures. Industry likelihood of approval from Phase II is much lower than 40%, which would support the broader point that CG's 40% for both stages is high (not verified).

0.7 × 0.3 = 0.21: arithmetic correct.** The 0.3 for P(III | weak signal) is an assumption with no support. Nothing in the critique shows that 0.3 is a better estimate than 0.57, the value implied by 0.40 ÷ 0.7.
E[p·RR] ≠ p·E[RR] when both depend on the true effect: VALID.** This is basic probability: the two differ by the covariance.

Winner's curse (realized effect below the planning value): PARTLY MISAPPLIED.** Winner's curse biases the estimated effect in a successful trial. Deaths averted depend on the true effect. Conditional on success, the true effect is selected upward, which is the opposite direction, as the critique acknowledges. The net direction is therefore ambiguous. This conflicts with the critique's header "Estimated Direction: decreases", and with its own "direction is ambiguous".
"Same linear effect on p_success as Critique 1": MINOR ERROR.** Critique 1 is about the RR term, not p_success.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
(strength: LOW–MEDIUM, direction: ambiguous, conditional on IIc definition)**
If the IIc endpoint is PK, dose or surrogate-based (a condition not yet verified), then P(IIc success) is likely high. Phase III then carries most of the risk, and the realistic joint probability could fall below 0.40. REMoxTB is a verified precedent for Phase II signals not translating. Because p_success and the true effect size are correlated, E[p·RR] ≠ p·E[RR]. Whether this raises or lowers the expected benefit needs a scenario analysis over a prior on the true effect. The winner's-curse point should be dropped or reframed as an effect-size selection argument. **UNGROUNDED:** P(IIc) = 0.7, P(III | weak signal) = 0.3, the 0.21 product, and the premise that IIc is dose-finding. **Correct** the "see Critique 2" reference to Critique 1 and fix the "Phase II→approval" wording.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: Baseline year is stale and the 5.5M figure is sensitive to it
original.hypothesis: If CG anchored on 2022 notifications (~7.5M), that was a post-COVID recovery year. WHO's later reports show notifications continuing to rise (~8.2M in 2023). The "8 years of decline" is then applied from a baseline that is already out of date. The thread notes there is no sensitivity analysis on baseline year.
original.mechanism: Moving the baseline from 7.5M to ~8.2–8.3M raises eligible_people_at_8y by ~9–11%, from ~5.5M to ~6.0–6.1M. Taken alone this is below the ±25% materiality bar. It is an upward, non-material correction. It matters mainly because it stacks with Critique 2.
suggested_evidence: Logical argument plus my recollection of WHO Global TB Reports (2023 and 2024 editions). I cannot give exact figures. This is a reconstruction concern and would need verification against the WHO reports.

evidence_found: The 2024 data point (8.3M, from the WHO Global TB Report 2025) post-dates the Investigator's recollection. It supports "upward, small."
The backlog caveat means the upward correction may be slightly overstated if the baseline is treated as a steady-state level.
caveats: 2022 notifications of ~7.5M:** VERIFIED.
WHO reported about 8.2 million newly diagnosed in 2023, up from 7.5 million in 2022.
~8.2M in 2023:** VERIFIED.
8.2 million was the highest single-year number since the mid-1990s, up from the previous record of 7.5M in 2022.
"Notifications continuing to rise":** PARTIALLY VERIFIED. They rose through 2023, then levelled off.
In 2024, 8.3 million were newly diagnosed and notified, similar to 8.2 million in 2023 and 17% above the pre-pandemic level of 7.1 million.
The better statement is that 2024 is a plateau at about 8.3M, which is 10.7% above 7.5M.
"2022 was a post-COVID recovery year":** VERIFIED. WHO says those diagnosed in 2022 and 2023 probably included a sizeable backlog of people whose diagnosis was delayed by COVID-related disruptions.
This applies to 2023 as well. Part of the 8.2M may be one-off backlog, so it is not a clean steady-state anchor either.
Arithmetic:** VERIFIED. 8.2/7.5 = +9.3% and 8.3/7.5 = +10.7%. Applied to 5.5M, that gives ~6.0–6.1M. The result is below the ±25% materiality bar.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
Same as stated, with these edits.
- Replace "continuing to rise" with "rose to 8.2M in 2023 and plateaued at 8.3M in 2024."
- Add the backlog caveat.
- Strength remains small, direction up (+9–11%).

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: A 2%/yr decline in notified case counts probably contradicts the observed trend; incidence rates fall slowly while counts do not
original.hypothesis: WHO's headline declines are in incidence *rates* per 100,000 (about 1–2%/yr in good pre-COVID years). Absolute case counts depend on population growth, which is large in the highest-burden countries (India, Nigeria, DRC, Pakistan, Philippines, Indonesia). Notified cases also reflect closing detection gaps (roughly 25% of incident cases are not notified), and WHO and national programmes are pushing active case-finding. If rate declines are roughly offset by population growth, absolute incident cases are roughly flat. If detection keeps improving, notifications could rise. CG applies a 2% annual decline to the count of cases. That is plausibly a different quantity from the one WHO reports as declining.
original.mechanism:
Scenario using my own arithmetic:
- Baseline 8.2M, flat for 8 years, × 0.96 × 0.90 → ~7.1M, about +29% versus 5.5M.
- A mild rise (+1%/yr) would give ~7.7M.
- A downside shock, such as the 2025 funding disruptions to TB programmes, could cut notifications. I cannot ground the size of that effect.

The 2%/yr figure therefore looks conservative for counts, and the error is probably in the upward direction (eligible ≈ 6.5–7.7M). Combined with Critique 1, this likely crosses the >25% threshold, but in the direction that improves cost-effectiveness.
suggested_evidence: WHO Global TB Report trends, which I recall showing global incident cases of ~10–11M and roughly flat in absolute terms since ~2015, with the rate falling ~8% over 2015–2023. I cannot cite exact values. Population growth is a logical argument. UNGROUNDED on specific numbers; needs verification.

evidence_found: WHO notes that the recovery in reported newly diagnosed cases in 2022–2024 first slowed increases in incidence, then reversed the upward trend.
Notifications and incidence estimates are therefore linked, which weakens any "independent" notification trend.
Counter-consideration: WHO's 2.4M gap bounds how much notifications can rise from detection alone. The ceiling is about +28% above 8.3M, and only in the unrealistic case of 100% detection.
caveats: Rates fall about 1–2%/yr:** VERIFIED. WHO describes declines of about 2% per year between 2010 and 2020, reversed by a 4.6% rise from 2020 to 2023.
The net reduction in the rate from 2015 to 2024 was 12.3% , which is about 1.4%/yr.
Rate down ~8% over 2015–2023:** VERIFIED.
The net reduction was 8.3%.
Counts are roughly flat while rates fall:** VERIFIED for the recent period, but "since 2015" is unconfirmed.
Incident cases fell 1% in 2024, from 10.8M to 10.7M, but remain above the 2020 level of 10.3M.
I did not retrieve a 2015 absolute figure.
Population growth drives counts:** VERIFIED in direction. WHO states most of the global increase in incident cases between 2022 and 2023 reflects population growth.
~25% of incident cases are not notified:** VERIFIED, and now somewhat better.
In 2024 about 2.4 million people were not diagnosed or not reported, and notifications were 78% of incidence.
In 2023 the gap was about 2.7 million, down from around 4 million in 2020 and 2021.
This supports "detection gaps are closing."
Notified counts are flat to rising, not falling 2%/yr:** VERIFIED. Notifications went from 7.1M in 2019 to 8.3M in 2024.
In the African Region they were 38% above 2019.
"CG applies a 2%/yr decline to counts":** UNVERIFIABLE. I have no CG source. This is the pivotal premise, so it should stay flagged.
Scenario arithmetic:** the arithmetic is correct.
The 6.5M lower bound corresponds to about −1%/yr.
Double-counting problem:** the +29% already includes Critique 1.
Flat counts remove 8 years of 2%/yr decline (0.98⁸ ≈ 0.85), which is worth +17.5% on its own.
The baseline update adds about +9% (1.093 × 1.175 ≈ 1.28).
Critique 2 alone is therefore about +17.5% for flat counts, or about +27% with +1%/yr growth.
Crossing the 25% bar needs Critique 1 or a rise in counts. The Investigator's wording ("combined with Critique 1") is right, but the +29% should not be presented as Critique 2's standalone effect.
2025 funding disruptions could cut notifications:** UNVERIFIABLE. My searches returned no data on the size of this effect, and the 2024 data pre-date it. It stays flagged as ungrounded.

Direction field "uncertain":** the text argues the error is probably upward, so the label is internally inconsistent. The evidence supports "likely increases," with downside risk from funding and from the backlog fading.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
Rate declines in WHO reporting are not the same as declines in case counts. Observed notifications rose from 7.5M (2022) to 8.3M (2024), and incident counts have been about flat (10.3–10.8M since 2020). If CG applies 2%/yr to counts, it likely understates the eligible population by roughly 17% (flat counts) to 27% (+1%/yr), before the baseline correction in Critique 1.
- Combined with Critique 1, eligible is about 6.5–7.7M.
- The CG-method premise and the funding-shock point stay flagged as UNGROUNDED.
- Strength: medium. Direction: up, with downside risk.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: "Adult DS notified" is not "eligible for the trial label": missing applicability filters
original.hypothesis:
The 5.5M appears to be adults with drug-susceptible TB, but a statin adjunct would likely be indicated only for a subset.
- **Extrapulmonary TB** is ~15% of notified cases. If the proposed mechanism and outcomes (culture conversion, relapse, lung pathology) are pulmonary, these patients are outside the evidence.
- **Clinically diagnosed (not bacteriologically confirmed) cases** are ~35–40% of notifications globally. These patients lack culture endpoints, and some may not have TB.
- **Exclusions typical of a statin trial:** HIV coinfection (~6–8% of cases; ART interactions), pregnancy, hepatic disease, existing statin use, and drug-interaction contraindications.
- **Isoniazid-resistant, rifampicin-susceptible TB** (Hr-TB, ~7% of cases) is classified as "DS" in some schemas but is treated with a different regimen. The 96% share may overstate trial-regimen-eligible patients.
original.mechanism:
Illustrative stack from my own multiplication:
- Pulmonary only: ×0.85 → ~4.7M.
- Add other filters (HIV, pregnancy, hepatic, Hr-TB), ×~0.85 → ~4.0M.
- Restrict to bacteriologically confirmed cases (×~0.62): ~2.5M.

Stacked with an overly conservative decline (Critique 2), this could net out to roughly the current figure. The filters should be modelled explicitly rather than implicitly. Applied alone and fully, they could push eligible below the 3.6M bar.
suggested_evidence: WHO Global TB Report for extrapulmonary share (~15–16%), bacteriological confirmation (~60–65%), and TB-HIV share. These are my recollections and should be verified. The statin exclusion list is my own inference from standard trial design and statin labelling, not from any specific protocol. Which filters apply depends on the trial design, which I have not seen.

evidence_found: Applying Critique 2's upside to these filters:
7.1M (flat, adjusted) × 0.85 × 0.85 = 5.1M. That is about −7% versus 5.5M, so it roughly nets out to the current figure, as the Investigator suggests.
Adding the confirmed-only restriction gives about 3.2M, below the 3.6M bar.
The conclusion therefore hinges on whether the label or trial requires bacteriological confirmation. That is the single most decision-relevant unknown.
Applying the filters to the regional mix makes this worse. India and South Asia have the highest extrapulmonary share, and Africa has the highest HIV share.
caveats: Extrapulmonary TB ~15%:** VERIFIED.
In 2024, 84% of notified cases were pulmonary and 16% extrapulmonary , and the 2023 figures were the same ( 84% and 16%
). Regional variation is large.
South-East Asia is 25% extrapulmonary , and
India and Bangladesh are above 20%.
The ×0.85 filter is therefore too lenient for India and South Asia, the biggest contributors.
Clinically diagnosed "~35–40% of notifications":** MISSTATED.
Of 6.9 million pulmonary cases in 2024, 64% were bacteriologically confirmed, up from 62% in 2023.
The 62–64% is a share of pulmonary cases, not of all notifications, so 36–38% of pulmonary cases are clinically diagnosed.
The stacked arithmetic does apply ×0.62 after the pulmonary filter, so it is consistent.
Of all notifications, confirmed pulmonary cases are only about 0.84 × 0.64 ≈ 54%.
HIV coinfection ~6–8%:** SLIGHTLY HIGH.
5.8% of incident cases in 2024 were among people living with HIV , and 6.1% in 2023.
Notified HIV-positive cases were
413,516 in 2024 , about 5% of 8.3M. A range of 5–7% is better. The share is concentrated in Africa, with over 50% in parts of southern Africa.
Hr-TB ~7%:** VERIFIED.
Hr-TB prevalence was estimated at 7.4% among new cases and 11.4% among previously treated cases.
Another source gives
7.1% of new cases. It is treated with a modified regimen including levofloxacin since 2018.

I did not verify how routinely Hr-TB is detected. Isoniazid DST is not routine, so many Hr-TB patients are probably in "DS" cohorts in practice. That blunts the filter's real-world effect but not a trial-eligibility one.

Pregnancy, hepatic disease, existing statin use, drug interactions:** UNVERIFIABLE. These are inference from standard trial design, as the Investigator says. The ×0.85 for "other filters" is also ungrounded. HIV plus Hr-TB alone gives about 0.87, so 0.85 is plausible but unsupported.
Stack arithmetic:** correct.
Restricting to bacteriologically confirmed cases is a trial-design choice. A label population may not carry it.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
Notified adult cases overstate the population that fits a pulmonary, trial-like label. Verified WHO figures:
- Extrapulmonary share is 16% globally and ~25% in South-East Asia.
- Pulmonary cases are 64% bacteriologically confirmed (the denominator is pulmonary, not all notifications).
- HIV is about 5–6%.
- Hr-TB is about 7%.

An illustrative stack gives 4.0M without confirmation and ~2.5M with it, before the upside from Critique 2. The statin-specific exclusions and the ×0.85 factor are the Investigator's own assumptions and are flagged as UNGROUNDED. Strength: medium. Standalone direction: down. Net direction when combined with Critique 2: uncertain.

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: Shorter and new regimens erode both the eligible population and the incremental benefit
original.hypothesis:
By ~2033, a meaningful share of DS-TB patients may be on regimens other than the 6-month HRZE the trial tests.
- WHO (2022) recommended a 4-month rifapentine–moxifloxacin regimen (HPMZ, from Study 31/A5349, Dorman et al., NEJM 2021) for people aged 12 and over.
- Other pipeline options include TRUNCATE-TB-type strategies (Paton et al., NEJM 2023, from my recollection) and bedaquiline-containing short regimens.

Consequences:
1. **Applicability:** a statin trial on HRZE does not establish efficacy on a rifapentine- or moxifloxacin-based backbone. Rifapentine is a stronger CYP3A4 inducer than rifampicin, so the interaction problem may worsen. Re-trialing on new backbones would add cost and time that the model may not count.
2. **Incremental value:** shorter, more potent regimens may lower baseline relapse and mortality. This leaves less room for an adjunct to add benefit, if the benefit is defined relative to standard-regimen outcomes.
3. **Mechanism:** if the statin's value is in shortening treatment, a 4-month regimen leaves less to shorten.
original.mechanism: If 20–40% of eligible patients are on non-trial regimens at the benefit horizon, effective eligible falls ~20–40%, from 5.5M to ~3.3–4.4M. That is at or near the 3.6M bar. If the effect size also shrinks on newer backbones, the effect compounds. The 20–40% adoption range is my own scenario and is not grounded in published projections. Programme uptake of HPMZ has so far been slow because of rifapentine supply and cost, so the low end is more likely than the high end.
suggested_evidence: Dorman et al. (NEJM 2021) and WHO 2022 guidance exist. The adoption forecast is UNGROUNDED, so this is an inference. The interaction claim for rifapentine and atorvastatin is pharmacological reasoning, not a cited study.

evidence_found: WHO's conditional recommendation, and its explicit reference to rifapentine availability, supports a slow-uptake scenario.
Adolescents aged 12–16 have three options: 4-month HPMZ, 4-month 2HRZ(E)/2HR, or standard 6-month.
The 4-month 2HRZ(E)/2HR regimen for non-severe paediatric TB is still rifampicin-based. It reduces duration, not the backbone.
Concerning "shortening" benefit: the 4-month 2HRZ(E)/2HR regimen applies only to non-severe TB in children under 16. It is not a general adult option.
No evidence was found on the effect of a statin adjunct on shorter regimens. This is a genuine gap.
caveats: WHO (2022) recommended a 4-month HPMZ regimen for people aged 12 and over: VERIFIED.**
The WHO 2022 DS-TB module recommends a 4-month isoniazid, rifapentine, moxifloxacin and pyrazinamide regimen for people aged 12 or older with pulmonary DS-TB.
It is a conditional recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence.
WHO also said that clinicians should weigh eligibility criteria, patient preference and local factors such as the availability of rifapentine.
This supports the supply and uptake caveat, though it does not quantify it.
Dorman et al., NEJM 2021 (Study 31/A5349): VERIFIED, with an incomplete check.**
I did not retrieve the paper directly. A trial protocol states that a four-month rifapentine regimen containing moxifloxacin was non-inferior to the standard 6-month regimen (Dorman et al., 2021).
A ClinicalTrials.gov reference list also carries the matching title, "Four-Month Rifapentine Regimens with or without Moxifloxacin for Tuberculosis."
Paton et al., NEJM 2023 (TRUNCATE-TB): VERIFIED, but MISCHARACTERISED as a "regimen" alternative.**
The citation is correct:
Paton NI et al., "Treatment Strategy for Rifampin-Susceptible Tuberculosis," N Engl J Med 2023;388(10):873-887.
It tested a management strategy, not a drop-in regimen.
An initial 8-week bedaquiline–linezolid regimen was noninferior to standard treatment for a composite clinical outcome at week 96.
The strategy includes monitoring and retreatment of relapses. A later exploratory analysis found all four 8-week regimens had lower efficacy than the standard 24-week regimen.
Its authors say that even the best 8-week bedaquiline-linezolid regimen should only be used within the TRUNCATE management strategy.
This makes TRUNCATE-TB a weaker candidate for displacing HRZE at scale by ~2033 than the critique implies. I found no WHO recommendation for it.
"Bedaquiline-containing short regimens" in the pipeline: PLAUSIBLE/VERIFIED as pipeline.**
Bedaquiline-containing regimens are being tested for DS-TB, for example the SimpliciTB bedaquiline-pretomanid-moxifloxacin-pyrazinamide trial.
There is also a Phase 2 trial of TBAJ-876 or bedaquiline with pretomanid and linezolid (NCT06058299).
These are Phase 2 or 2c. None is a recommended DS-TB standard of care.
"Rifapentine is a stronger CYP3A4 inducer than rifampicin": UNVERIFIED, and probably wrong as stated.**

I found no source in my searches. My background understanding, which I could not re-check this session, is that rifapentine is usually described as a CYP3A4 inducer of similar or somewhat lower potency than rifampicin, not a stronger one.
What does survive: both are strong rifamycin inducers, so a statin interaction concern applies to HPMZ as well. The "may worsen" wording should be dropped.
Slow HPMZ uptake because of rifapentine supply and cost: PLAUSIBLE, UNVERIFIED.**
One 2025 abstract notes that the high rifapentine dose may limit use in clinical practice, particularly in patients with comorbidities.
That is a clinical limitation, not a supply or cost finding. I found no programme-level uptake data.
20–40% adoption scenario: UNGROUNDED, as the Investigator admits.** The arithmetic is correct: 5.5M × 0.6–0.8 = 3.3–4.4M.
The 5.5M eligible figure and the 3.6M bar** come from the CEA source materials, which I do not have. I could not check them.
critique.revised_hypothesis:
- **Hypothesis:** By the benefit horizon, some DS-TB patients may be on the WHO-recommended 4-month HPMZ regimen, which includes rifapentine and moxifloxacin in place of rifampicin and ethambutol. 
This applies to people aged 12 or older.
 A statin trial on HRZE may not transfer to that backbone.
- **Retained:**
  1. Applicability: the evidence is HRZE-specific.
  2. Incremental value: shorter regimens leave less room for a duration-shortening adjunct.
  3. Rifamycin interaction concerns would likely apply to rifapentine as well as rifampicin. The direction and size of any difference is unverified.
- **Corrections:**
  - TRUNCATE-TB is a strategy trial with bedaquiline–linezolid, not a WHO-endorsed standard regimen, so it is a weaker driver of displacement.
  - Bedaquiline-based DS-TB regimens remain in Phase 2 or 2c.
- **Flagged UNGROUNDED:** the 20–40% adoption range and the slow-uptake claim. The drop to 3.3–4.4M is arithmetic on an assumed range.
- **Strength:** medium, direction uncertain. The adoption share is the key unknown. The "at or near 3.6M" conclusion depends wholly on the assumed range.

target_parameters.name: Smaller incremental benefit from a duration-shortening adjunct

original.thread_name: Eligible population and the future TB landscape
original.title: M72/AS01E and other incidence shocks are likely not large enough by year 8–10, but should be modelled
original.hypothesis:
The Phase III of M72/AS01E (started 2024, ~20,000 participants, results expected late 2020s from my recollection of Gates MRI materials) follows a Phase IIb (Tait et al., NEJM 2019) that reported ~50% efficacy against progression to pulmonary TB in already-infected adults. If Phase III succeeds, licensure could come ~2028–30, with rollout starting thereafter.

The 30–50% incidence reduction that would be material is unlikely by 2033–35:
- Rollout is slow. Adolescent and adult programmes need Gavi financing and new delivery platforms.
- Vaccine impact accrues gradually, mostly by preventing progression in already-infected people.

My own estimate is a 5–15% reduction in incidence by 2033–35, which on its own would not cross the threshold. LSHTM-type models (e.g. Harris et al.) project larger impacts mostly in the 2040s. I cannot cite a specific figure from them.

The vaccine effect matters more over the *benefit horizon*. If atorvastatin benefit accrues across many years after adoption, a vaccine could reduce the eligible pool by 30–50% in the later years. CG's constant 5.5M "eligible at 8y" ignores the downward trajectory after that point.
original.mechanism: Effect on eligible at year 8: –5 to –15%, i.e. ~4.7–5.2M. If the benefit horizon extends beyond ~15 years, average eligible over that horizon could be ~20–35% lower, depending on how the horizon is modelled. I cannot determine this without seeing how the CEA treats post-adoption years (**magnitude uncertain, requires CEA sensitivity analysis**). The probability of vaccine success should be weighted separately (the Phase IIb efficacy estimate was in a small, selected population).
suggested_evidence: Tait et al. (NEJM 2019) for the Phase IIb. The Phase III timeline is from my recollection of Gates MRI. The modelling is a general recollection that I cannot cite precisely. UNGROUNDED on the specific impact numbers.

evidence_found: Global M72 demand-forecast work and country models exist and could ground the rollout assumptions. I did not extract specific numbers.
An M72-specific South Africa model and India models exist (
49.7% efficacy over 3 years in previously sensitised adolescents and adults as the input). These would be better sources than Harris 2019 for a sensitivity analysis.
Efficacy was assessed only in IGRA+ individuals, and its uncertainty and duration of protection (10 years is an assumed value in one model) add further uncertainty to any projected incidence effect.
caveats: Phase III started 2024: VERIFIED.**
In March 2024, M72 went into phase 3 trials.
The registered trial is NCT06062238, run by the Gates Medical Research Institute ( ongoing registrational efficacy trial. ).
~20,000 participants: PARTIALLY VERIFIED.** Sources vary.
Nature reports around 26,000 participants across seven countries.
A design paper models
18,000 IGRA-positive participants for the primary analysis, with the full trial larger once other groups are added.
~20,000 is not wrong for the IGRA+ core, but ~26,000 is the better-supported total.
Results "late 2020s": PLAUSIBLE.** The design paper projects a 90% probability of accruing 110 events within 3.5 to 4 years.
With enrolment starting in 2024, a primary readout near 2028 is consistent. Licensure around 2028–30 is therefore plausible but unconfirmed.
Phase IIb efficacy was in a small, selected population: VERIFIED.**
It enrolled
3,573 HIV-negative adults aged 18–50 who were IGRA-positive.
It rested on
39 primary-analysis cases (13 in the vaccine group, 26 on placebo).
The Investigator's caution about probability-weighting is well founded.
Vaccine impact mostly via preventing progression in the already-infected: VERIFIED as the efficacy basis, with modelling nuance.**
Phase IIb efficacy was measured only in infected people. LSHTM modellers note that a pre- and post-infection vaccine had a much greater impact on 2050 incidence than a post-infection-only vaccine.
That supports the idea that impact accrues gradually.
An analysis of the trial found that the most plausible models needed protection against at least two of the three routes to active TB.
So the mechanism is not settled.

Slow rollout needing Gavi financing: PLAUSIBLE.** A recent M72 demand-forecast paper includes an "upside" scenario with higher efficacy, more global funding (Gavi and others) and faster rollout than the base case.
This implies the base case assumes slower and more constrained rollout.
